items.title: Quiz
items.text:
Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

Q1. A 3-person startup with 5 microservices needs to go live this week. Which deployment option has the shortest time-to-live?

  • A. AWS EKS — production-grade from day one
  • B. Railway or Fly.io — connect GitHub, push, done
  • C. AWS ECS Fargate — container-native, no nodes to manage
  • D. AWS Lightsail — simplest AWS option
Answer

B — Railway or Fly.io.

Railway and Fly.io can deploy a Dockerized Spring Boot application in minutes with zero infrastructure configuration. EKS requires days of setup (VPC, node groups, IAM roles, add-ons, ingress controllers); ECS Fargate still requires VPC, IAM task roles, ALB, and ECR configuration; Lightsail is simple but still needs an image pushed to a registry and a manual container service setup. When time-to-live is the constraint, a PaaS that builds straight from the repository wins.

Q2. What is the main operational difference between ECS Fargate and EKS for a team of 10 developers?

  • A. ECS Fargate requires managing EC2 node groups; EKS does not
  • B. ECS Fargate is serverless — no nodes to manage; EKS requires managing node groups, networking add-ons, and the full Kubernetes API surface
  • C. EKS is cheaper at 10 services because the control plane is shared across workloads
  • D. ECS Fargate supports GitOps via ArgoCD natively; EKS does not
Answer

B — ECS Fargate is serverless; EKS requires managing node groups and the full K8s API surface.

With ECS Fargate, AWS provisions and patches the underlying compute — you define a task (CPU, memory, container image, env vars) and AWS runs it. With EKS, you pay for the control plane (~$73/month) and manage node groups yourself: instance types, AMI updates, node draining during upgrades, and all Kubernetes add-ons. At 10 developers, the ECS operational simplicity typically outweighs the loss of the Kubernetes ecosystem.

Q3. The EKS control plane alone costs about $73/month. A student's 3-service project should use EKS. True or false — and why?

  • A. True — EKS is the industry standard and every project should use it for resume value
  • B. True — EKS scales to zero so it is cost-effective for small projects
  • C. False — EKS costs ~\(73/month for the control plane alone, plus ~\)61/month for a minimal node group (2 × t3.medium), totalling far more than the entire cost of running 3 services on Railway, Fly.io or Lightsail
  • D. False — EKS is only available to enterprise AWS accounts
Answer

C — False. EKS control plane + minimum node group exceeds the total cost of simpler alternatives.

The EKS control plane is $0.10/hour × 730 hours ≈ $73/month before a single container runs. A minimal node group (2 × t3.medium) adds about $61/month, and a load balancer and a small RDS database bring the class's cost model to roughly $180/month — against roughly $15–25/month for the same three services on Fly.io, Railway or a Lightsail VM (October 2026 list prices, us-east-1). (The course project uses EKS anyway because its goal is to learn Kubernetes.) Beyond cost, EKS requires significant operational knowledge (IAM roles for service accounts, VPC CNI networking, ingress controller setup) that distracts from learning the application-level concepts the course targets.

Q4. What is K3s and when would you choose it over AWS EKS?

  • A. K3s is a Kubernetes dashboard; choose it when you need better visibility into EKS clusters
  • B. K3s is a lightweight Kubernetes distribution (< 100 MB binary) that implements the same API as upstream K8s; choose it for on-premises deployments, edge devices, or cost-sensitive environments where cloud-managed control planes are not an option
  • C. K3s is a managed Kubernetes service from Rancher, competing directly with EKS on AWS infrastructure
  • D. K3s is a Kubernetes version that removes CRD support to reduce complexity
Answer

B — K3s is a lightweight, full-API-compatible Kubernetes distribution for on-prem, edge, or cost-sensitive deployments.

K3s runs the complete Kubernetes API in a binary under 100 MB, replacing etcd with SQLite by default and stripping out cloud-provider integrations. You would choose K3s over EKS when you need Kubernetes on bare-metal servers (a university data center, a factory floor, a Raspberry Pi cluster), when internet connectivity is unreliable, or when the ~$73/month EKS control plane fee is unjustifiable. The trade-off is that you own all operations — upgrades, backups, and HA setup — with no AWS managed support.

Q5. In 2026 a student team wants App Runner-style simplicity — "give a container image, get an HTTPS URL" — for the store's order service on AWS. What should they use?

  • A. AWS App Runner — it is still the recommended entry point for new AWS accounts
  • B. Amazon ECS Express Mode — one call with an image and two IAM roles creates a Fargate service, an ALB with HTTPS, auto scaling and a URL, all as ordinary ECS resources in their account
  • C. Amazon EKS — it is the only AWS service that gives an HTTPS URL for a container
  • D. AWS Lambda — package the Spring Boot service as a function
Answer

B — Amazon ECS Express Mode.

AWS closed App Runner to new customers on 30 April 2026 (existing customers keep it, without new features) and recommends ECS Express Mode as the replacement. Express Mode has no extra charge — you pay for the Fargate tasks, the load balancer and the other resources it creates — and because everything it creates is visible and editable in your account, the team can later "graduate" to full ECS Fargate without migrating. Unlike App Runner, it does not build from source: the CI pipeline must build and push the image to ECR first.

Q6. A service deployed on Fly.io in the São Paulo region (gru) serves users in Europe. What Fly.io capability can reduce latency for European users?

  • A. Fly.io automatically caches all API responses globally — no configuration needed
  • B. You can deploy the same container to additional Fly.io regions (e.g., lhr for London, ams for Amsterdam) with a single flag, and Fly's Anycast routing directs each user to the nearest region
  • C. Fly.io uses CloudFront to serve responses from European edge nodes automatically
  • D. Fly.io compresses all responses before transmitting, reducing effective latency
Answer

B — Deploy to additional regions; Fly.io's Anycast routing directs users to the nearest instance.

Fly.io assigns each application an Anycast IP address. When a European user connects, their request is routed by BGP to the nearest Fly edge node that runs your container — typically lhr (London) or ams (Amsterdam). Adding regions is one command, e.g. fly scale count 3 --region gru,lhr,ams. The trade-off: stateless services scale globally with zero effort, but stateful services (databases, sessions) require deliberate replication or global consistency strategies — the classic Fly Postgres is an app you operate yourself, and the newer Managed Postgres removes that work at a higher fixed price.

Q7. The store is deployed on Lightsail container services: the gateway has the public endpoint, and it must call the account service and an RDS Postgres database that lives in a normal AWS VPC. Which statement is correct?

  • A. Lightsail containers share the AWS default VPC, so both calls work with no configuration
  • B. Every Lightsail container service must be public; the gateway calls account through its public URL, and RDS is unreachable from Lightsail
  • C. The gateway can reach account through its private domain (account.service.local), but reaching RDS in a VPC requires enabling Lightsail VPC peering with the account's default VPC
  • D. Lightsail requires an App Runner VPC Connector to reach both account and RDS
Answer

C — Private domain for Lightsail-to-Lightsail; VPC peering for RDS.

Lightsail does not use standard AWS VPC networking. Each container service gets one public endpoint plus a private domain <service-name>.service.local, reachable from other Lightsail resources in the same Region — enough for gateway → account. Resources outside Lightsail, such as an RDS instance in a regular VPC, are reachable only after enabling Lightsail VPC peering with the default VPC of the Region, a step many tutorials skip. There are no security groups or network policies to fine-tune either, which is one reason teams outgrow Lightsail.

Q8. A team is growing from 5 to 25 engineers and from 8 to 40 microservices. Currently on Railway. What is the most important factor deciding whether to migrate to ECS Fargate or EKS?

  • A. The number of microservices — ECS handles up to 30, EKS handles more
  • B. Whether the team has (or plans to hire) a dedicated platform or DevOps engineer who can own Kubernetes operations — ECS Fargate is the right answer without one, EKS becomes viable with one
  • C. The programming language — EKS is required for Java services, ECS for Node.js
  • D. Monthly budget — ECS Fargate is always cheaper than EKS regardless of scale
Answer

B — The presence of a dedicated platform engineer is the decisive factor.

At 40 microservices, both ECS Fargate and EKS are technically capable. The real question is operational ownership. EKS requires someone who understands Kubernetes networking (CNI, services, ingress), manages node group upgrades, configures RBAC, installs and maintains add-ons (Karpenter, ArgoCD, external-secrets-operator), and responds to cluster incidents. Without a dedicated platform engineer, these tasks fall on feature developers, slowing product delivery. ECS Fargate covers most needs of a typical microservice system with no control-plane fee and no nodes to operate — and is the right answer for most teams at this scale unless GitOps, multi-tenancy, or cross-cloud portability are hard requirements.

Q9. The class's cost model estimates about $71/month for the store's three services on ECS Fargate (low configuration). Roughly $30 of that is the Application Load Balancer and $14 is RDS. What does this tell you?

  • A. The estimate is wrong — compute is always the largest line of a cloud bill
  • B. At small scale, fixed per-hour resources (load balancer, database, NAT gateway, EKS control plane) dominate the bill, and they are charged even with zero traffic
  • C. Load balancers are only charged per request, so the $30 disappears when nobody uses the store
  • D. Moving the same services to EKS would remove the load balancer cost
Answer

B — Fixed costs dominate at small scale.

Three small Fargate tasks (0.25 vCPU / 0.5 GB) cost about $27/month; the ALB's hourly fee, capacity units and public IPv4 addresses cost about $30, and the smallest RDS instance about $14 — all billed by the hour whether or not requests arrive. EKS would add a $73 control plane and still need a load balancer. This is why fixed-fee platforms lose at three services and win at fifty, and why forgotten NAT gateways, load balancers and clusters are the classic surprise on a student's bill.

Q10. A 4-person team runs 6 services on Railway. Deploys are smooth, the monthly bill is predictable, and no customer has complained about performance. A developer proposes migrating to EKS "because that's what big companies use". What is the best response?

  • A. Migrate now — it is cheaper to move before the system grows
  • B. Migrate to EKS but keep Railway as a backup
  • C. Stay: there is no concrete pain point. Keep the services portable (containers, configuration in environment variables, Postgres) and define the signals that would justify moving — e.g., need for AWS services, compliance, private networking or many teams
  • D. Move to raw EC2 VMs to get maximum control
Answer

C — Stay, and define the migration triggers.

Each migration should be driven by a concrete pain point, not by speculation or résumé value. EKS would add a fixed control-plane fee, node operations and Kubernetes expertise the team does not need yet — hours of platform work that ship no feature. Keeping the application 12-factor makes a later move a deployment exercise rather than a rewrite, so waiting costs little.

Q11. Running K3s on a single $24/month VM gives the store the full Kubernetes API for a fraction of the EKS price. What do you give up compared with EKS?

  • A. The Kubernetes API — K3s uses its own manifest format
  • B. Nothing — K3s on one VM is equivalent to EKS
  • C. A managed, highly available control plane: on one VM the control plane is a single point of failure, and upgrades, datastore backups and certificates become your job
  • D. The ability to run Spring Boot containers
Answer

C — The managed, highly available control plane.

K3s is a CNCF-certified distribution, so your Deployments, Services and Ingresses work unchanged. What EKS's $0.10/hour buys is a control plane that AWS runs across several Availability Zones, patches and backs up. With K3s on one VM, losing the VM loses the cluster and every workload on it; self-hosting moves the work to you, not just the cost away.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
Imagine the store you will build in this course running as a single Spring Boot application with one PostgreSQL database on one machine. It is simple to reason about — until traffic grows beyond what that machine can handle, or the machine dies and the whole store goes down with it. The moment you split the work across several machines (a gateway, an account service, an order service, a database, a cache, a message broker), you have built a distributed system, and a new class of problems appears.

Distributed systems represent a computing paradigm where multiple independent computers collaborate to achieve a common goal, appearing as a single coherent system to the end-user3. Unlike centralised systems where all processing occurs on one machine, distributed systems span networks and leverage interconnected nodes (a node is any independent computer or process taking part in the system) to handle data storage, computation, and communication.

This architecture underpins modern cloud platforms (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure), large-scale applications (social networks, e-commerce), and scientific simulations. The foundational challenge is that nodes operate independently, communicate only by passing messages, and have no shared clock — making coordination a non-trivial engineering problem.

Learning objectives

By the end of this class you should be able to:

  • Explain what makes a system distributed and why partial failure, unreliable networks and the absence of a global clock make it hard.
  • Identify the 8 fallacies of distributed computing in a concrete design, such as a call between two microservices.
  • Explain how logical clocks (Lamport) order events without a shared physical clock.
  • Choose between consistency and availability for a given data domain using CAP and PACELC.
  • Describe how Raft elects a leader and replicates a log with majority quorums, and size a cluster for a given number of failures.
  • Compare strong consistency (quorums, consensus) with eventual consistency (LWW, vector clocks, CRDTs).

items.title: Roadmap
items.text:
1. This overview — what a distributed system is, why we build them, what they cost, and the three root problems (partial failure, unreliable network, no global clock).
  2. CAP Theorem — the consistency-versus-availability choice during a network partition, and its PACELC extension.
  3. Consensus & Algorithms — how nodes agree on a value despite failures: FLP, failure models, Paxos, Raft, quorums and CRDTs.
  4. Quiz — check your understanding.

items.title: Slides
items.text: Click the slides and use ← → to move through them; F goes full screen and P opens the presenter view, with the notes. Open the slides in a new tab

items.title: Our store is a distributed system
items.text:
A single click on "Place order" in the store already crosses the network several times. Follow the request:

flowchart LR
    user([Browser]) -->|POST /orders| gw[Gateway]
    gw -->|validate token| auth[Auth service]
    gw -->|forward| order[Order service]
    order -->|check stock| product[Product service]
    product -->|cached price| redis[(Redis)]
    order -->|INSERT order| pg[(PostgreSQL)]
    order -->|OrderCreated| kafka[[Kafka]]

Each arrow is a message over the network, and each box is a process that can fail on its own. If the product service is slow, the order service waits; if Kafka is down, the order may be stored but the event never published. Nothing in this picture shares memory or a clock — the services cooperate only by exchanging messages. That is exactly the definition of a distributed system, and it is why the rest of this class matters for the project.

items.title: Classification
items.text:
Distributed systems can be classified along several axes:

Dimension Option A Option B Hardware/software uniformity Homogeneous — all nodes run the same stack Heterogeneous — diverse hardware and OS Coupling Tightly coupled — high interdependence, shared memory Loosely coupled — communicate via messages, independent lifecycle Topology Client-server — hierarchical, servers hold resources Peer-to-peer — egalitarian, all nodes share resources

Web applications follow the client-server model (browsers request from servers). File-sharing systems like BitTorrent follow peer-to-peer. Most microservice architectures occupy the loosely-coupled middle ground: our store is heterogeneous (Java services, a Python notification service, PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka), loosely coupled (services talk over HTTP and Kafka) and client-server (the browser calls the gateway, the gateway calls the services).

items.title: Advantages
items.text:
Benefit How Horizontal scalability Add nodes instead of upgrading a single machine. Cassandra scales to petabytes by adding nodes seamlessly. Fault tolerance Replication across nodes keeps the system running despite individual failures. Google Spanner uses synchronous cross-datacenter replication. Resource sharing Idle capacity from many machines is pooled. Folding@home aggregates CPU cycles for scientific workloads. Parallelism Tasks are divided and processed concurrently. MapReduce (Hadoop) exemplifies this for big-data analytics. Latency reduction Nodes placed near users reduce round-trip time. CDNs like Akamai serve content from the nearest edge location.

In the store, horizontal scalability is what Hands-on 7 does with Nginx in front of several replicas of a service, and latency reduction is what the Redis cache of Hands-on 8 provides.

items.title: Disadvantages
items.text: Challenge Root cause Complexity Coordination, synchronisation, and distributed state are hard to reason about and implement correctly. Network overhead Messages can be delayed, lost, or duplicated. Every failure mode must be handled explicitly. Consistency vs availability During a network partition, a replicated data store cannot be both consistent and available — see the CAP Theorem. Expanded attack surface More nodes mean more entry points. Byzantine faults (malicious nodes) require dedicated protocols. Operational cost Debugging, monitoring, and deploying distributed systems requires specialised tooling (Prometheus, Kubernetes, distributed tracing).

items.title: The 8 Fallacies of Distributed Computing
items.text:
L. Peter Deutsch and colleagues at Sun Microsystems2 listed the assumptions developers commonly make when building distributed systems — all of them wrong (the list had seven items in 1994; James Gosling added the eighth, the network is homogeneous, in 1997):

Fallacy Reality In the store The network is reliable Packets are dropped, links fail, cables are cut The call from order to product fails halfway Latency is zero Network round-trips add milliseconds; cross-region adds hundreds Five sequential calls of 40 ms each make a 200 ms checkout Bandwidth is infinite Transferring large payloads saturates links Returning the whole catalogue in one response The network is secure Traffic must be encrypted and authenticated at every hop Services trust any caller inside the cluster Topology doesn't change Nodes go up and down; IPs change; services are rescheduled A Kubernetes pod is rescheduled with a new IP There is one administrator Multiple teams, multiple cloud accounts, multiple policies Another team changes a firewall rule Transport cost is zero Serialisation, compression, and egress fees are real JSON parsing and cross-zone traffic on the cloud bill The network is homogeneous Different systems speak different protocols and encodings Java services, a Python service, Kafka's binary protocol

Design for failure, not against it

These fallacies share a common root: treating the network as a reliable local function call. The correct posture is to assume failure will happen and design every interaction to degrade gracefully.

items.title: The three root problems
items.text: Almost every difficulty in this course traces back to three facts.

items.title: 1. Partial failure
items.text: On a single machine, a program either works or crashes as a whole. In a distributed system, part of the system can fail while the rest keeps running: the product service is down but the gateway and the order service are fine. Each component must decide what to do when one of its dependencies stops answering.

items.title: 2. An unreliable network: slow or dead?
items.text:
When the order service sends a request and gets no reply, it cannot know what happened. Consider the possibilities:

sequenceDiagram
    participant O as Order service
    participant P as Product service
    O->>P: reserve 1 unit of product 42
    Note over O,P: request lost? P crashed? reply lost? P just slow?
    O-->>O: timeout after 2 s
    O->>P: retry: reserve 1 unit of product 42
    P-->>O: OK (but was the first one applied too?)

From the caller's point of view, a lost request, a crashed server, a lost reply and a very slow server all look the same: silence. The only practical tool is a timeout — after a deadline, assume failure. But a timeout does not tell you whether the operation was executed, so a retry may apply it twice. That is why operations that may be retried must be idempotent (applying them twice has the same effect as applying them once — for example, by sending a unique request id that the server deduplicates). Timeouts, retries with backoff and circuit breakers are covered in Resilience Patterns.

items.title: 3. No global clock
items.text: Each machine has its own quartz clock, and clocks drift: two servers synchronised with NTP (Network Time Protocol) can still disagree by milliseconds, and much more after a misconfiguration or a VM pause. So you cannot reliably order two events on different machines by comparing their wall-clock timestamps — an order created "at 10:00:00.120" on one node may actually have happened after a cancellation stamped "10:00:00.150" on another.

items.title: Time and ordering: logical clocks
items.text:
Leslie Lamport1 observed that, for most purposes, we do not need the real time of events — we need their order, and specifically the happened-before relation (→):

  • if a and b happen in the same process and a comes first, then a → b;
  • if a is the sending of a message and b its receipt, then a → b;
  • if a → b and b → c, then a → c.

Two events where neither happened-before the other are concurrent: neither could have influenced the other.

A Lamport clock is a counter kept by each process, updated with three rules:

  1. Before each local event, increment the counter.
  2. When sending a message, attach the current counter value.
  3. When receiving a message with value t, set the counter to max(local, t) + 1.
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Order service
    participant B as Kafka consumer
    participant C as Notification
    Note over A: create order (L=1)
    A->>B: OrderCreated (L=2)
    Note over B: receive: max(0,2)+1 = 3
    Note over C: local event (L=1)
    B->>C: SendEmail (L=4)
    Note over C: receive: max(1,4)+1 = 5

The guarantee is: if a → b then L(a) < L(b). The converse is not true — a smaller Lamport timestamp does not prove that one event caused the other. Vector clocks fix this by keeping one counter per process; comparing two vectors tells you whether one event happened before the other or whether they are concurrent. They are used to detect conflicting writes in replicated databases (see Eventual consistency).

Where you will meet ordering in the course

Kafka does not use wall-clock time to order messages: it assigns each message a monotonically increasing offset inside a partition, so all consumers see the same order for that partition (Hands-on 9). Raft uses a logical counter called a term to tell old leaders from new ones (Consensus).

Do not order events by System.currentTimeMillis() across machines

Comparing timestamps produced by different servers is a classic source of bugs, for example in "last write wins" conflict resolution: a node with a fast clock silently wins every conflict. Use a single authority for ordering (a database sequence, a Kafka partition offset) or logical clocks.

items.title: Topics covered
items.text:
• CAP Theorem

    The central trade-off in distributed data stores: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance cannot all be guaranteed simultaneously. Understand CP, AP, and CA system classes — and the PACELC extension.

    CAP Theorem

  • Consensus & Algorithms

    How distributed nodes reach agreement despite failures. Covers Paxos, Raft, quorum systems, failure models (crash-stop, Byzantine), the FLP impossibility result, and eventual consistency.

    Consensus & Algorithms

items.title: Connections
items.text:
• Microservices — splitting the store into services is what turns it into a distributed system.
  • Event-Driven Architecture and Hands-on 9 — asynchronous messaging with Kafka, ordered by partition offsets.
  • Reliability — timeouts, retries, circuit breakers: designing for partial failure.
  • Hands-on 7 and Hands-on 8 — horizontal scaling behind a load balancer, and a Redis cache.
  • Hands-on 10 — distributed tracing, to see one request crossing many services.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• A distributed system is a set of independent nodes that cooperate only by exchanging messages and have no shared clock; our store is one as soon as it has more than one service.
  • We distribute for scalability, fault tolerance and latency — and pay in complexity, network failures and operational cost.
  • The 8 fallacies are all false: design every remote call for failure.
  • A caller cannot tell a slow node from a dead one: use timeouts, and make retried operations idempotent.
  • Physical clocks drift; order events with a single authority or with logical clocks (Lamport, vector clocks).

  1. LAMPORT, L. Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System. CACM, 1978. ↩

  2. DEUTSCH, P. Fallacies of Distributed Computing, 1994. ↩

  3. VAN STEEN, M.; TANENBAUM, A. S. Distributed Systems, 4th ed., 2023. ↩

items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation. Try to answer before revealing.

items.title: Foundations
items.text:
Q1. The order service calls the product service to reserve one unit of stock and gets no reply within its 2-second timeout. What can it safely conclude?

  • A. The product service has crashed and must be restarted
  • B. The reservation was not applied, so it is safe to retry without any precaution
  • C. Nothing certain — the request may have been lost, applied with the reply lost, or still be in progress; a retry must be idempotent
  • D. The network is partitioned, so the order service must switch to CP mode
Answer

C — Nothing certain; retries must be idempotent.

A lost request, a crashed server, a lost reply and a very slow server all look the same to the caller: silence. The timeout only says "I stopped waiting". If the reservation was actually applied and the reply was lost, a naive retry reserves the unit twice. Making the operation idempotent (for example, with a unique request id that the server deduplicates) makes the retry safe.

Q2. Using Lamport clocks, process B has counter 3 and receives a message stamped 7. What is B's counter after the receive event?

  • A. 3
  • B. 4
  • C. 7
  • D. 8
Answer

D — 8.

On receipt, the rule is max(local, received) + 1 = max(3, 7) + 1 = 8. This guarantees that the receive event gets a larger timestamp than the send event, so "happened-before" is always reflected in the timestamps. Note the converse does not hold: a smaller Lamport timestamp does not prove causality — vector clocks are needed for that.

items.title: CAP Theorem
items.text:
Q3. What does the P in CAP stand for, and why is it non-negotiable in any real distributed system?

  • A. Performance — slow systems are considered unavailable
  • B. Persistence — data must survive node restarts
  • C. Partition Tolerance — the system continues operating despite network partitions
  • D. Predictability — responses must arrive within a bounded time
Answer

C — Partition Tolerance.

Network partitions — where messages between nodes are lost or delayed — happen in any real distributed system due to hardware failures, congestion, or physical distance. Because partitions cannot be prevented, the practical design choice is between C (refuse requests during partition) and A (continue serving, possibly stale data).

Q4. A distributed database refuses all reads during a network partition to avoid returning stale data. Which CAP category does it belong to?

  • A. CA — Consistent and Available
  • B. CP — Consistent and Partition-Tolerant
  • C. AP — Available and Partition-Tolerant
  • D. None — it violates all three properties simultaneously
Answer

B — CP.

By refusing reads during a partition, the system prioritises consistency (no stale data) over availability. Once the partition heals, service resumes. ZooKeeper and etcd are classic CP examples.

Q5. Which of the following systems are typically classified as AP (Available and Partition-Tolerant)?

  • A. Apache ZooKeeper and etcd
  • B. PostgreSQL and MongoDB
  • C. Apache Cassandra and DNS
  • D. Redis and SQLite
Answer

C — Apache Cassandra and DNS.

Both continue serving requests during partitions, accepting that responses may be temporarily stale (eventual consistency). ZooKeeper and etcd are CP; PostgreSQL with synchronous replication and MongoDB with its default majority writes behave as CP. A single-node Redis or SQLite is not replicated at all, so CAP does not really apply to it — it sits in the "CA" corner only because there is no second node to be partitioned from.

Q6. The PACELC theorem extends CAP. What does the ELC part address that CAP ignores?

  • A. Even when a partition heals, the system must re-elect a leader before serving
  • B. Even without a partition, the system must choose between Latency and Consistency
  • C. Every lost connection requires a Checkpoint before normal operation resumes
  • D. Eventual consistency is always preferred over strong consistency at low load
Answer

B — Even without a partition: Latency vs Consistency trade-off.

CAP only describes behaviour during a partition. PACELC adds that even in normal operation, systems must trade off between lower latency (serve quickly, risk slightly stale reads) and stronger consistency (wait for replication agreement before responding). Cassandra is PA/EL; MongoDB with majority writes is PC/EC.

Q7. A payment service must never allow a double charge. A network partition occurs between the payment node and the replication node. Which design is correct?

  • A. Use an AP store — availability ensures the payment always goes through
  • B. Use a CA store — the single-node guarantee prevents concurrency issues
  • C. Use a CP store — refuse the request during the partition rather than risk an inconsistent state
  • D. Use an AP store with last-write-wins — timestamps prevent duplicates
Answer

C — CP store.

For financial transactions, correctness is non-negotiable. A CP store refuses to process the payment during the partition (the customer gets an error, not a double charge). An AP store might process the payment on two nodes simultaneously before the partition heals, creating a duplicate transaction that cannot be safely undone. Last-write-wins (D) would silently discard one of the conflicting writes, and depends on clocks that drift.

Q8. In which scenario is a CA system (Consistent and Available) actually achievable?

  • A. In a three-node cluster with synchronous replication
  • B. In a geographically distributed system with dedicated links
  • C. Only on a single-machine system or tightly controlled LAN with no partitions possible
  • D. Never — CA is theoretically impossible
Answer

C — Single-machine or tightly controlled LAN.

CA only works when partitions genuinely cannot occur — which is only realistic for a single server or a local area network under strict control. In any internet-connected or geographically distributed deployment, P is effectively mandatory, leaving the real choice between C and A.

Q9. In PACELC terms, how would you classify a system that favours low latency during normal operation and availability during a partition?

  • A. PC/EC
  • B. PA/EC
  • C. PC/EL
  • D. PA/EL
Answer

D — PA/EL.

PA = during a Partition, favours Availability. EL = Else (normal operation), favours Latency. Apache Cassandra is the canonical PA/EL system — it always responds quickly and accepts eventual consistency in both scenarios.

items.title: Consensus Algorithms
items.text:
Q10. What does the FLP Impossibility Theorem prove about distributed consensus?

  • A. Consensus is impossible in any system with more than one node
  • B. In a purely asynchronous system where even one process may crash, no deterministic algorithm can guarantee that consensus is always reached
  • C. Leader election always terminates within a fixed number of rounds
  • D. Byzantine failures make consensus impossible even with synchronous networks
Answer

B — No guaranteed termination in an async system with ≥1 faulty node.

FLP (Fischer, Lynch, Paterson, 1985) proves this fundamental limit: some unlucky ordering of delays can keep any deterministic algorithm undecided forever. Real algorithms respond by assuming partial synchrony (delays are eventually bounded) or by using randomisation. Paxos and Raft never violate safety, and use timeouts as a proxy for failure detection to make progress.

Q11. In Raft, what event triggers a new leader election?

  • A. The current leader sends a resign message to the cluster
  • B. A majority of followers vote to remove the current leader
  • C. A follower's election timeout expires without receiving a heartbeat from the current leader
  • D. The cluster detects that the leader's log has diverged from followers
Answer

C — Follower election timeout expires.

Each follower maintains a randomised election timeout. If no heartbeat arrives before it expires, the follower assumes the leader has crashed and starts a new election by incrementing the term and requesting votes. Randomised timeouts prevent multiple followers from starting elections simultaneously.

Q12. A team runs etcd on 4 nodes "to be safer than 3". How many node failures can the 4-node cluster tolerate while still accepting writes?

  • A. 1 — the same as a 3-node cluster
  • B. 2 — half of the nodes
  • C. 3 — any single surviving node can serve writes
  • D. 0 — an even number of nodes cannot elect a leader
Answer

A — 1.

A write needs a majority: ⌊4/2⌋ + 1 = 3 nodes. With 2 nodes down only 2 remain, which is not a majority. So 4 nodes tolerate ⌊(4-1)/2⌋ = 1 failure — the same as 3 nodes, with one more machine that can fail. That is why consensus clusters use odd sizes (3 or 5). An even cluster can still elect a leader (D is false); it just gains nothing.

Q13. Which formula guarantees that any read quorum overlaps with any write quorum, ensuring you always read the latest write?

  • A. W > N / 2
  • B. R > N / 2
  • C. W = R = N
  • D. W + R > N
Answer

D — W + R > N.

If write quorum W plus read quorum R exceeds total replicas N, at least one node that acknowledged the write must also participate in any read quorum. This overlap ensures the latest write is always visible in a quorum read, forming the basis of systems like Dynamo and Cassandra's tunable consistency (for example, QUORUM reads and writes with N = 3: 2 + 2 > 3).

Q14. Two replicas of a G-Counter CRDT hold [4, 1, 0] and [2, 3, 0] (one slot per node). What is the counter's value after they merge?

  • A. 5 — the larger of the two totals
  • B. 7 — the element-wise maximum [4, 3, 0], summed
  • C. 10 — the sum of both totals
  • D. It depends on which replica merged last
Answer

B — 7.

The G-Counter merge takes the element-wise maximum of the slots: [max(4,2), max(1,3), max(0,0)] = [4, 3, 0], whose sum is 7. Because each node only increments its own slot, the maximum of a slot is its latest value; summing the two totals (C) would double-count, and the merge is commutative and idempotent, so the order of merges does not matter (D is false).

items.title: CAP Theorem
items.text:
Suppose the product service of our store keeps its data in PostgreSQL replicated on two nodes, one in each data centre, so that the store survives the loss of a whole site. One afternoon the link between the two sites goes down, but both nodes are still alive and still receiving requests. A customer on site B asks for the stock of product 42, which was just updated on site A. Node B has two options: answer with what it has (possibly stale) or refuse to answer until it can talk to A again. There is no third option — and this is exactly what the CAP theorem formalises.

The CAP Theorem, proposed by Eric Brewer in 2000 and formally proven by Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch in 20021, states that a distributed system that replicates data across nodes cannot simultaneously guarantee all three of the following properties3:

CAP theorem Three overlapping circles: Consistency, Availability and Partition tolerance. The overlaps are CP and AP, the two real choices, and CA, which only exists without partitions. The centre, all three at once, is impossible. Consistency every read sees the latest write Availability every request gets a non-error answer Partition tolerance works while the network is split CP ZooKeeper, etcd AP Cassandra, DNS CA no partitions (single node) all three: impossible Partitions will happen, so the real choice is CP or AP — during a partition.

items.title: The three properties
items.text:
Consistency (C) : Every read returns the most recent write, or an error. All nodes see the same data at the same time — equivalent to linearisability (the system behaves as if there were a single copy of the data and every operation took effect at one instant). In a consistent system, it is impossible to read stale data.

Availability (A) : Every request received by a non-failing node receives a non-error response — even if the response may not contain the most recent write.

Partition Tolerance (P) : The system continues to operate despite arbitrary network partitions — message drops or delays between nodes. A partition splits the nodes into groups that can still run but cannot talk to each other. Partitions are a fact of life in any real distributed network; hardware failures, congestion, and physical distances all cause them.

Partition Tolerance is not optional

In any real-world distributed system, network partitions will happen. The practical choice is therefore between C and A during a partition — not whether to include P.

The C in CAP is not the C in ACID

In ACID database transactions, consistency means "the transaction leaves the data valid according to the constraints" (foreign keys, CHECK, invariants). In CAP, consistency means linearisability: every replica answers as if there were only one copy. A single PostgreSQL server is ACID-consistent; the question CAP asks only appears when there are replicas.

items.title: A partition, step by step
items.text:
The same scenario played twice: once by a CP system and once by an AP system.

sequenceDiagram
    participant CA as Client A
    participant N1 as Node 1 (majority side)
    participant N2 as Node 2 (isolated)
    participant CB as Client B
    Note over N1,N2: 3 replicas: Node 1 and Node 3 can still talk, Node 2 is cut off
    CA->>N1: write stock[42] = 0
    N1-xN2: replicate (link is down)
    N1-->>CA: OK
    CB->>N2: read stock[42]
    alt CP: choose consistency
        N2-->>CB: error: cannot reach majority
    else AP: choose availability
        N2-->>CB: stock[42] = 5 (stale)
    end
    Note over N1,N2: partition heals, replicas sync

Neither answer is "wrong": the CP node refuses rather than lie; the AP node answers with the best value it has. Which one is acceptable depends on the data, not on the technology.

items.title: CP — Consistent and Partition-Tolerant
items.text:
During a partition, the system refuses requests rather than returning potentially stale data. When the partition heals, consistency is restored before serving again.

Examples: Apache ZooKeeper, etcd, PostgreSQL with synchronous replication, MongoDB (with majority write concern and primary reads, the defaults).

Use when: correctness is non-negotiable — financial transactions, inventory systems, identity stores.

flowchart LR
    CA(["Client A"]) -->|"1 · write stock = 0"| A[("Node A<br/>stock = 0")]
    A -.-x|"2 · replicate ✗ partition"| B[("Node B<br/>stock = 5")]
    CB(["Client B"]) -->|"3 · read stock"| B
    B -->|"4 · error: unavailable"| CB

items.title: AP — Available and Partition-Tolerant
items.text:
During a partition, every node continues to respond, but nodes may diverge and return different data. After the partition heals, the system converges to a consistent state (eventual consistency).

Examples: Apache Cassandra, Amazon DynamoDB, CouchDB, DNS.

Use when: availability matters more than momentary accuracy — shopping carts, social media feeds, search indexes.

flowchart LR
    CA(["Client A"]) -->|"1 · write stock = 0"| A[("Node A<br/>stock = 0")]
    A -.-x|"2 · replicate ✗ partition"| B[("Node B<br/>stock = 5")]
    CB(["Client B"]) -->|"3 · read stock"| B
    B -->|"4 · stock = 5 (stale)"| CB
    A ==>|"5 · partition heals: sync"| B

items.title: CA — Consistent and Available
items.text: Assumes no partitions, which is only realistic for single-machine systems or tightly controlled LANs. Not a practical category for distributed systems.

items.title: Comparison table
items.text:
CP AP CA Consistency ✅ Always ❌ Eventually ✅ Always Availability ❌ During partition ✅ Always ✅ Always Partition tolerance ✅ ✅ ❌ (unrealistic) Trade-off Reject requests during partition Return possibly stale data Only works on single node Examples ZooKeeper, etcd, PostgreSQL (sync replication) Cassandra, DynamoDB, DNS Single-node RDBMS

CP and AP are labels for a configuration, not for a product

Most databases let you tune the trade-off per request: Cassandra reading and writing with QUORUM behaves much more like a CP system, and PostgreSQL serving reads from an asynchronous replica can return stale data. Many real systems are, strictly speaking, neither fully CP nor fully AP5. Ask "how is it configured, and what happens to my requests during a partition?" rather than "is this database CP or AP?".

items.title: The PACELC extension
items.text:
The CAP theorem only addresses the partition scenario. PACELC (Daniel Abadi, 2010)2 extends it by asking: even when there is no partition, what is the trade-off?

flowchart LR
    Q{"Is there a<br/>partition?"} -->|"yes · P"| PAC{"Availability<br/>or Consistency?"}
    PAC -->|A| PA["PA: answer, maybe stale"]
    PAC -->|C| PC["PC: refuse or wait"]
    Q -->|"no · E (else)"| ELC{"Latency<br/>or Consistency?"}
    ELC -->|L| EL["EL: answer before<br/>the replicas confirm"]
    ELC -->|C| EC["EC: wait for<br/>the replicas"]

The reason is replication: to be consistent, a write must wait for other replicas to acknowledge it (a network round-trip, possibly to another region); to be fast, it must answer before they do — and accept that a replica may briefly lag behind.

System Partition behaviour Normal behaviour Classification Cassandra Favours A Favours L (low latency) PA/EL DynamoDB Favours A Favours L PA/EL MongoDB (majority writes) Favours C Favours C PC/EC PostgreSQL (synchronous replication) Favours C Favours C PC/EC

PACELC4 is more useful than CAP for making day-to-day database choices, because most of the time there is no partition — yet the latency/consistency trade-off is always present.

PACELC in the store: read replicas

A common way to scale reads is to add an asynchronous read replica to PostgreSQL and send GET /products to it. Reads become faster and the primary is relieved — the EL choice. The price is replication lag: right after an admin updates a price on the primary, the replica may still return the old one for a few milliseconds (or seconds under load). The Redis cache of Hands-on 8 makes the same choice: a cached product can be stale until its TTL expires.

items.title: Practical implications for system design
items.text:
E-commerce product catalogue → AP : Showing a product as in-stock when it has just gone out of stock is acceptable. A brief period of stale data does not harm correctness.

Shopping cart → AP : Adding an item to a cart that temporarily diverges across replicas is fine; the cart can reconcile on checkout.

Payment processing → CP : A double charge or missed debit cannot be reconciled after the fact. Consistency is required.

User authentication → CP : A revoked token must be immediately invalid across all nodes. Stale auth state is a security vulnerability.

Most systems mix both

A single application can use an AP store (Cassandra) for user activity logs and a CP store (PostgreSQL) for financial records. Choose per data domain, not per application.

Common mistakes

  • "We chose CA." If the data is on more than one machine, partitions can happen; CA only means "we never thought about what happens during one".
  • Treating CAP as a permanent property. The C/A choice only applies during a partition; the rest of the time the trade-off is latency (PACELC).
  • Forgetting the cache. Adding Redis in front of a CP database makes those reads AP-like: the cache can serve stale data.

items.title: Connections
items.text:
• Consensus & Algorithms — how CP systems such as etcd actually stay consistent: majorities and Raft.
  • Hands-on 8 — a Redis cache, an explicit choice of latency over consistency.
  • Event-Driven Architecture — asynchronous events make services eventually consistent with each other.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• CAP: when the network partitions, a replicated store must choose between consistency (refuse) and availability (answer, maybe stale).
  • P is not optional, so the real choice is C or A during a partition; CA only exists on a single node.
  • CAP's C is linearisability — not ACID's C.
  • PACELC: even without a partition, replication forces a choice between latency and consistency.
  • Choose per data domain and per configuration: payments and auth CP, catalogue and cart AP.

  1. GILBERT, S.; LYNCH, N. Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services. ACM SIGACT News, 2002. ↩

  2. ABADI, D. Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design. IEEE Computer, 2012. ↩

  3. CAP Theorem — Wikipedia ↩

  4. PACELC Theorem ↩

  5. KLEPPMANN, M. Please stop calling databases CP or AP, 2015. ↩

items.title: Consensus & Algorithms
items.text:
When the store runs on Kubernetes (Hands-on 5), the whole state of the cluster — which pods exist, which image each Deployment runs, which Secrets are defined — lives in etcd. A production cluster runs three or five etcd members so that the cluster survives the loss of a machine. But replication brings a question: if two kubectl apply commands arrive at two different members at the same moment, and one member then crashes, which version is the truth, and how do the survivors agree on it without a referee? Answering that question is the consensus problem.

Consensus is the problem of getting a group of distributed nodes to agree on a single value — despite messages being delayed, lost, or reordered, and despite some nodes failing. It is the foundational primitive for leader election, distributed locks, replicated state machines, and consistent configuration stores.

A replicated state machine is the most common use: every node starts in the same state and applies the same commands in the same order (a log), so every node ends in the same state. Consensus is what makes all nodes agree on the next entry of the log.

A correct consensus algorithm must guarantee two kinds of property:

Safety ("nothing bad happens") : All nodes that decide, decide the same value, and that value was actually proposed by someone.

Liveness ("something good eventually happens") : Every non-faulty node eventually decides.

items.title: Why consensus is hard: the FLP Impossibility
items.text:
The FLP Impossibility Theorem (Fischer, Lynch, Paterson, 1985)1 proves that in a purely asynchronous distributed system (no upper bound on message delays or processing time) with even a single node that may crash, no deterministic algorithm can guarantee that consensus is always reached. Some execution — an unlucky ordering of delays — can keep the algorithm undecided forever.

The implication is that every practical consensus algorithm makes a trade-off:

  • It assumes partial synchrony: the network may misbehave for a while, but eventually delays become bounded — and it only guarantees progress (liveness) during those "good" periods, or
  • It uses randomisation, so that it terminates with probability 1, or
  • It weakens the problem (for example, accepting that it may block forever in adversarial conditions).

Paxos and Raft take the first route: they never violate safety, even when the network is chaotic, and make progress whenever the network is "well-behaved enough".

Real systems handle this by using timeouts as a proxy for failure detection — accepting that a slow node looks indistinguishable from a crashed one (see the three root problems).

items.title: Failure models
items.text:
Before choosing a consensus algorithm, you must know what failures to tolerate:

Model What a faulty node does Tolerance cost Crash-stop The node halts and never recovers Easiest to handle — a majority of N nodes can tolerate ⌊(N-1)/2⌋ failures Crash-recovery The node halts but may restart with persistent state Requires durable logs; algorithms must handle rejoining nodes Byzantine The node behaves arbitrarily — incorrect messages, equivocation, malice Hardest — requires 3f+1 nodes to tolerate f Byzantine failures

Most datacenter algorithms assume crash-stop or crash-recovery. Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT) is used in blockchain and safety-critical systems.

items.title: Majorities: why clusters have 3 or 5 nodes
items.text:
Paxos, Raft and ZooKeeper all rely on the same idea: a decision is valid only if a majority (more than half) of the N nodes agrees. Any two majorities of the same cluster share at least one node, so two conflicting decisions can never both collect a majority — that shared node would have to vote for both.

Cluster size N Majority (⌊N/2⌋ + 1) Failures tolerated (⌊(N-1)/2⌋) 1 1 0 2 2 0 3 2 1 4 3 1 5 3 2 7 4 3

Use an odd number of nodes

Going from 3 to 4 nodes adds cost and one more machine that can fail, but tolerates no extra failure. That is why etcd, ZooKeeper and Consul clusters are sized 3 or 5. A 2-node cluster is worse than a single node: losing either node stops it.

A majority also protects against split brain — two parts of a partitioned cluster both believing they are in charge. With 5 nodes split 3/2, only the side with 3 can form a majority:

flowchart LR
    subgraph maj ["Majority side (3 of 5)"]
        n1[Node 1 leader] --- n2[Node 2]
        n2 --- n3[Node 3]
    end
    subgraph min ["Minority side (2 of 5)"]
        n4[Node 4] --- n5[Node 5]
    end
    n3 -.-|partition| n4
    maj -->|"can elect and commit"| ok([keeps serving writes])
    min -->|"cannot reach 3 votes"| ko([rejects writes])

items.title: Paxos
items.text:
Paxos2, introduced by Leslie Lamport (published in 1998, explained more simply in 2001), is the classic consensus algorithm for crash failures in asynchronous networks. It operates in two phases and tolerates up to ⌊(N-1)/2⌋ failures with N nodes. Nodes play three roles: proposers suggest values, acceptors vote on them, and learners find out the decided value.

sequenceDiagram
  participant P as Proposer
  participant A1 as Acceptor 1
  participant A2 as Acceptor 2
  participant A3 as Acceptor 3

  Note over P,A3: Phase 1 — Prepare
  P->>A1: Prepare(n)
  P->>A2: Prepare(n)
  P->>A3: Prepare(n)
  A1-->>P: Promise(n, -)
  A2-->>P: Promise(n, -)
  A3-->>P: Promise(n, -)

  Note over P,A3: Phase 2 — Accept
  P->>A1: Accept(n, value)
  P->>A2: Accept(n, value)
  P->>A3: Accept(n, value)
  A1-->>P: Accepted
  A2-->>P: Accepted

Phase 1 (Prepare): The proposer picks a unique ballot number n and sends it to the acceptors. Each acceptor promises not to accept any proposal with a lower number, and replies with the highest-numbered proposal it has already accepted, if any (the - in the diagram means "none").

Phase 2 (Accept): Once a majority has promised, the proposer sends Accept(n, value). The value is not free: if any promise carried a previously accepted value, the proposer must propose the value of the highest-numbered one; only if none did can it propose its own. Acceptors accept if they have not since promised a higher ballot. The value is chosen once a majority has accepted it — in the diagram, two of three acceptors are enough.

The rule "adopt the previously accepted value" is what makes Paxos safe: once a value may have been chosen, every later proposer is forced to propose that same value.

Paxos is notoriously difficult to implement correctly. It does not specify leader election, log compaction, or membership changes — each production implementation must solve these separately.

items.title: Raft
items.text:
Raft3 (Ongaro and Ousterhout, 2014) was designed explicitly for understandability. It decomposes the consensus problem into three relatively independent sub-problems:

  1. Leader election — one node becomes leader; all writes go through it.
  2. Log replication — the leader appends entries to its log and replicates them to followers.
  3. Safety — a committed entry is never overwritten; leaders only commit after a quorum acknowledges.
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Follower
  Follower --> Candidate : election timeout
  Candidate --> Leader : wins election (majority vote)
  Candidate --> Follower : sees higher term
  Leader --> Follower : sees higher term

Terms act as logical clocks (see Time and ordering): each term begins with an election, and there is at most one leader per term. A node that receives a message from a higher term immediately steps down to follower.

items.title: Leader election sequence
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant N1 as Node 1 (Candidate)
  participant N2 as Node 2 (Follower)
  participant N3 as Node 3 (Follower)

  Note over N1,N3: Term 1 — leader is silent, election timeout fires on Node 1
  N1->>N1: increment term to 2, vote for self
  N1->>N2: RequestVote(term=2, lastLogIndex=5)
  N1->>N3: RequestVote(term=2, lastLogIndex=5)
  N2-->>N1: VoteGranted(term=2)
  N3-->>N1: VoteGranted(term=2)
  Note over N1: majority (2/3) — becomes Leader for term 2
  N1->>N2: AppendEntries(term=2, heartbeat)
  N1->>N3: AppendEntries(term=2, heartbeat)

A candidate wins the election only if it receives votes from a majority of nodes and its log is at least as up-to-date as the voters' logs (the election restriction). This ensures the new leader already holds all committed entries. Each node votes for at most one candidate per term.

Election timeouts are randomised (the Raft paper suggests 150–300 ms): if all followers timed out at the same instant, they would all become candidates, split the votes and nobody would win. With random timeouts, one node usually times out first and wins before the others start.

Raft is used in etcd (the key-value store underpinning Kubernetes), CockroachDB, and Consul.

items.title: Log replication
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant L as Leader
  participant F1 as Follower 1
  participant F2 as Follower 2

  C->>L: Write x=5
  L->>F1: AppendEntries(x=5)
  L->>F2: AppendEntries(x=5)
  F1-->>L: OK
  F2-->>L: OK
  Note over L: Majority acknowledged — commit
  L-->>C: Success

The leader only responds to the client after a majority of nodes (counting itself) have durably written the entry. Because any future leader must win votes from a majority, and any majority contains at least one node holding the entry, a committed entry survives the failure of any minority of nodes.

Try it

The Raft visualization4 lets you stop nodes and watch a new election, and The Secret Lives of Data5 walks through Raft step by step.

items.title: Quorum systems
items.text:
A quorum is the minimum number of nodes that must participate in an operation for it to be valid. Quorums are the mechanism that makes read/write pairs consistent without requiring every node to participate. Raft's majority is one kind of quorum; leaderless databases such as Cassandra and DynamoDB use read and write quorums directly.

For a system with N replicas:

Operation Requirement Write quorum (W) W nodes must acknowledge the write Read quorum (R) R nodes must respond to the read Consistency condition W + R > N

When W + R > N, every read quorum overlaps with every write quorum — at least one node in the read set has the latest write.

Example: N=5, W=3, R=3 → W + R = 6 > 5 ✅

Counter-example: N=3, W=1, R=1 → W + R = 2 ≤ 3 ❌ — a read may hit only the replica that missed the write.

Cassandra's tunable consistency exposes W and R as per-request parameters (QUORUM, ALL, ONE), letting the caller trade off between consistency and latency.

Setting (N = 3) W R W + R > N? Effect write ONE, read ONE 1 1 ❌ fastest; reads may be stale write QUORUM, read QUORUM 2 2 ✅ reads see the latest acknowledged write; tolerates 1 node down write ALL, read ONE 3 1 ✅ fast reads, but a single node down blocks every write

W + R > N is necessary, not sufficient

The overlap guarantees that a read contacts a node with the latest write, but edge cases remain: two concurrent writes, a write that succeeded on fewer than W nodes and was reported as failed, or "sloppy" quorums that accept writes on substitute nodes during failures. Quorum databases are therefore usually described as offering tunable consistency, not linearisability.

items.title: Eventual consistency and CRDTs
items.text:
Eventual consistency is the guarantee made by AP systems: if no new updates are made, all replicas will eventually converge to the same value. It does not specify when.

Strategies for convergence:

  • Last-Write-Wins (LWW): Each write carries a timestamp; the highest timestamp wins. Simple but risks losing concurrent writes — and depends on clocks that drift (see No global clock).
  • Vector clocks: Track causality between operations; detect concurrent writes for explicit conflict resolution (see logical clocks).
  • CRDTs (Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types):6 Data structures mathematically designed so that concurrent updates always merge without conflict. Examples: counters, sets (add-only), registers.

The trick behind a CRDT is a merge function that is commutative, associative and idempotent: replicas can exchange their state in any order, any number of times, and still end up equal. The simplest one is the grow-only counter (G-Counter), for example "number of views of a product" counted on several nodes:

// A G-Counter CRDT: each node increments only its own slot
class GCounter {
    private final long[] counts;   // one slot per node
    private final int me;          // this node's index

    GCounter(int nodes, int me) { this.counts = new long[nodes]; this.me = me; }

    void increment() { counts[me]++; }

    long value() { return Arrays.stream(counts).sum(); }

    // merge = element-wise max: order and repetition do not matter
    void merge(GCounter other) {
        for (int i = 0; i < counts.length; i++)
            counts[i] = Math.max(counts[i], other.counts[i]);
    }
}

If node 0 counted 3 views ([3, 0]) and node 1 counted 2 ([0, 2]), both merge to [3, 2] and report 5 — no update is lost, and no coordination was needed. Using a single shared number with "last write wins" would have reported 3 or 2.

CRDTs are used in Riak's data types, Redis Enterprise Active-Active databases and collaborative-editing libraries such as Automerge and Yjs. Amazon's Dynamo shopping cart (2007) used a related idea: divergent cart versions, detected with vector clocks, were merged by set union.

items.title: In practice: use, don't build
items.text:
Tool Role Consensus algorithm etcd Key-value store, Kubernetes config Raft Apache ZooKeeper Coordination, leader election ZAB (Zookeeper Atomic Broadcast, Paxos-derived) Consul Service discovery, distributed locks Raft Apache Kafka Distributed log, messaging KRaft (Raft-based); ZooKeeper mode was removed in Kafka 4.0 (2025)

The Kafka setup of Hands-on 9 runs Kafka 4 in KRaft mode: there is no ZooKeeper container — the coordination runs inside Kafka itself, on its own Raft quorum.

Pitfalls

  • Do not implement Paxos or Raft yourself for an application. Delegate to a proven system: etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul, or the database (a SELECT … FOR UPDATE, a unique constraint, an advisory lock).
  • Consensus is not free. Every write waits for a majority round-trip and goes through a single leader, so consensus systems store small, critical data (configuration, leadership, locks) — not your product catalogue.
  • A lock is not a guarantee. A process holding a distributed lock can pause (garbage collection, VM migration) and wake up after its lease expired, while another process now holds the lock. Protect the resource with a fencing token (a number that increases with each lock grant and is checked by the storage).

items.title: Connections
items.text:
• CAP Theorem — consensus-based stores (etcd, ZooKeeper) are the classic CP systems.
  • Hands-on 5 — Kubernetes keeps its whole state in etcd, replicated with Raft.
  • Hands-on 9 and Event-Driven Architecture — Kafka replicates partitions with a leader per partition.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Consensus makes nodes agree on one value (or one log order) despite failures; it underlies leader election, locks and replicated state machines.
  • FLP: in a fully asynchronous system no deterministic algorithm always terminates; real algorithms keep safety always and rely on timeouts for liveness.
  • Majorities overlap, which prevents split brain; N nodes tolerate ⌊(N-1)/2⌋ crash failures, so use 3 or 5 nodes.
  • Raft: randomised election timeouts, one leader per term, commit after a majority acknowledges; used by etcd, Consul and Kafka (KRaft).
  • Quorums need W + R > N; AP systems converge with LWW, vector clocks or CRDTs with a commutative, idempotent merge.

  1. FISCHER, M.; LYNCH, N.; PATERSON, M. Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process. JACM, 1985. ↩

  2. LAMPORT, L. Paxos Made Simple. ACM SIGACT News, 2001. ↩

  3. ONGARO, D.; OUSTERHOUT, J. In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft). USENIX ATC, 2014. ↩

  4. Raft Visualization — interactive animation of leader election and log replication. ↩

  5. The Secret Lives of Data: Raft — an engaging narrative visualization of Raft's mechanics and design decisions. ↩

  6. SHAPIRO, M. et al. Conflict-free Replicated Data Types. SSS, 2011. ↩

items.title: Event-Driven Architecture
items.text:
Synchronous REST works well when the caller needs an immediate answer. But when an order is placed, the system might need to notify 5 downstream services — email, inventory, fraud detection, shipping, analytics. Calling them all synchronously before returning to the user creates a latency cliff and a coupling explosion. Event-driven architecture solves this with a fundamentally different contract: publish an event, and let interested parties react asynchronously.

Learning objectives

By the end of this class you should be able to:

  • Decide when a call between two services should be a synchronous request or an asynchronous event.
  • Explain how Kafka organises data in topics, partitions and offsets, and how consumer groups give both fan-out and load sharing.
  • Choose a message key that preserves the ordering the business needs, and configure producer durability (acks, replication).
  • Explain at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery, and design an idempotent consumer.
  • Apply the transactional outbox and the saga pattern to keep data consistent across services without distributed transactions.
  • Compare event sourcing and CQRS with a classic CRUD model, and handle poison messages with a dead letter queue.

items.title: Slides
items.text: Click the slides and use ← → to move through them; F goes full screen and P opens the presenter view, with the notes. Open the slides in a new tab

items.title: Why Event-Driven?
items.text:
Two delivery models side by side: the synchronous chain forces the producer to wait for every downstream service before it can respond; the async model returns immediately after publishing.

Synchronous Call ChainAsynchronous Event Publish

The producer must wait for every downstream service to complete before returning a response to the client. Latency accumulates, and a single slow (or failing) dependency stalls the entire request.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Client
    participant OrderService
    participant EmailService
    participant InventoryService
    participant FraudService

    Client->>+OrderService: POST /orders
    OrderService->>+EmailService: sendConfirmation()
    EmailService-->>-OrderService: ok
    OrderService->>+InventoryService: reserveStock()
    InventoryService-->>-OrderService: ok
    OrderService->>+FraudService: checkFraud()
    FraudService-->>-OrderService: ok
    OrderService-->>-Client: 201 Created

The producer publishes a single event and immediately returns. Each downstream service consumes the event independently — in parallel, on its own schedule, without the producer knowing or caring.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant OrderService
    participant Kafka
    participant EmailService
    participant InventoryService
    participant FraudService

    Client->>+OrderService: POST /orders
    OrderService->>Kafka: publish OrderCreated
    OrderService-->>-Client: 202 Accepted
    Kafka-->>EmailService: OrderCreated (async)
    Kafka-->>InventoryService: OrderCreated (async)
    Kafka-->>FraudService: OrderCreated (async)
Concern Synchronous (REST) Asynchronous (Event) Latency Sum of all calls Only producer latency Coupling Producer knows all consumers Producer knows none Resilience One slow consumer blocks all Consumer failures are independent Throughput Limited by slowest dependency Consumers scale independently Debugging Simple request trace Requires distributed tracing Consistency Strong (synchronous) Eventual

The simulation below illustrates what happens to queue depth when the consumer cannot keep up with the producer — and what happens when it catches up.
