There are usually two timeouts on an HTTP call: the connect timeout (how long to wait to open the TCP connection) and the read timeout (how long to wait for the response once connected). Configure both.

Timeouts on the store's Feign client

# order-service application.yaml (Spring Cloud OpenFeign)
spring:
  cloud:
    openfeign:
      client:
        config:
          product:              # the @FeignClient name
            connect-timeout: 500    # ms
            read-timeout: 1000      # ms

If the product service takes more than one second, the order service gets an exception instead of a blocked thread, and can decide what to do next.

Timeouts are only the first step

A timeout on its own just converts a hang into a fast error. Combine it with a retry policy (below) for transient failures, and with a circuit breaker and a fallback for longer outages.

items.title: Retry with Exponential Backoff
items.text:
A retry re-attempts a failed request after a waiting period. Retries are appropriate for transient failures — brief network blips, momentary service restarts, or transient resource exhaustion — where the same request is likely to succeed on a subsequent attempt.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Service

    C->>+S: Request (attempt 1)
    S-->>-C: 503 Service Unavailable
    Note over C: wait 1 s
    C->>+S: Request (attempt 2)
    S-->>-C: 503 Service Unavailable
    Note over C: wait 2 s
    C->>+S: Request (attempt 3)
    S-->>-C: 200 OK ✓

items.title: Exponential backoff
items.text:
Retrying immediately on failure is dangerous: if many clients all retry simultaneously after a service restart, the resulting spike can overwhelm the recovering service — a thundering herd. Exponential backoff spaces retries out:

\[ \text{wait}_n = \min\left(c \cdot 2^n,\ \text{max\_wait}\right) \] Attempt Formula Wait (c = 1 s) 1 \(1 \cdot 2^0\) 1 s 2 \(1 \cdot 2^1\) 2 s 3 \(1 \cdot 2^2\) 4 s 4 \(1 \cdot 2^3\) 8 s 5 \(1 \cdot 2^4\), capped 16 s (= max_wait of 16 s) 6+ capped at max 16 s

items.title: Jitter
items.text:
Even with exponential backoff, clients that all failed at the same moment will retry at the same moments — a synchronised wave of retries. Adding a random jitter breaks this synchronisation:

\[ \text{wait}_n = \min\left(c \cdot 2^n,\ \text{max\_wait}\right) + \text{random}(0,\ \text{jitter\_cap}) \]

Marc Brooker's analysis at AWS2 compared several variants and recommends full jitter, which randomises the entire wait instead of adding a small random amount:

\[ \text{wait}_n = \text{random}\left(0,\ \min\left(c \cdot 2^n,\ \text{max\_wait}\right)\right) \]

With 1,000 clients failing at the same instant, full jitter spreads their retries uniformly over the interval instead of sending 1,000 requests at exactly t = 1 s, 2 s, 4 s.

items.title: What to retry — and what not to
items.text:
Response Retry? Why Connection refused, connection reset, timeout Yes Typical transient failure 503 Service Unavailable, 429 Too Many Requests Yes, with backoff (respect Retry-After if present) The server is asking you to come back later 500 Internal Server Error Maybe, once Often a bug that will fail again 400, 401, 403, 404, 422 No The request itself is wrong; retrying cannot fix it

Retry amplification

Retries multiply load exactly when the system is weakest. If the gateway, the order service and the product client each retry 3 times, one user click can become 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 calls to a struggling product service. Retry at one layer only (usually the one closest to the failing dependency), cap the number of attempts, and stop retrying when the circuit breaker is open.

Do not retry non-idempotent operations

Retrying a POST /orders that creates a new order may create duplicates. Only retry operations that are idempotent (GET, PUT, DELETE) or that are explicitly designed for retry safety (idempotency keys, deduplication tokens).

An operation is idempotent when doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. The common way to make a POST safe to retry is an idempotency key: the client generates a unique ID (e.g. a UUID) per logical operation and sends it in a header; the server stores the keys it has already processed and, on a repeated key, returns the stored result instead of creating a second order.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant O as Order service
    participant DB as Postgres
    C->>O: POST /orders (Idempotency-Key: k-42)
    O->>DB: key k-42 seen? no → insert order + key
    O--xC: 201 Created (response lost)
    C->>O: retry POST /orders (Idempotency-Key: k-42)
    O->>DB: key k-42 seen? yes
    O-->>C: 201 Created (same order, no duplicate)

items.title: Circuit Breaker
items.text:
The circuit breaker3 is named by analogy with the electrical component: when the current load exceeds safe limits, the breaker trips and interrupts the circuit. In software, when a downstream service failure rate exceeds a threshold, the circuit breaker opens and immediately rejects calls to that service — without attempting the network call at all.

This prevents the calling service from wasting threads and connections on a dependency that is known to be unavailable.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Closed

    Closed --> Open : failure rate exceeds threshold\n(e.g. > 50% errors in last 10 calls)
    Open --> HalfOpen : wait timeout expires\n(e.g. 30 seconds)
    HalfOpen --> Closed : probe request succeeds
    HalfOpen --> Open : probe request fails

Closed (normal operation) : Requests pass through. The breaker counts successes and failures. If the failure rate crosses the configured threshold, the breaker trips to Open.

Open (failing fast) : All requests are rejected immediately with an error — no network call is made. This protects the caller's resources and gives the downstream service time to recover. After a configured wait timeout, the breaker moves to Half-Open.

Half-Open (testing recovery) : A limited number of probe requests are allowed through. If they succeed, the downstream service has recovered and the breaker closes. If they fail, the breaker returns to Open.

items.title: Configuration knobs
items.text:
Parameter Typical value Effect Failure threshold 50% of last 10–20 calls Sensitivity to failures Wait timeout 30–60 seconds How long the service gets to recover Half-Open probe count 3–5 requests How cautiously to test recovery Slow call threshold 2× normal P99 Treat slow calls as failures

Spring Boot: the Resilience4j library4 implements all of these patterns with @CircuitBreaker, @Retry, @Bulkhead, @RateLimiter and @TimeLimiter annotations (dependency io.github.resilience4j:resilience4j-spring-boot3 plus spring-boot-starter-aop).

Circuit breaker and retry around the product call

OrderService.javaapplication.yaml 
@CircuitBreaker(name = "product", fallbackMethod = "priceFallback")
@Retry(name = "product")
public ProductOut findProduct(String id) {
    return productController.findById(id).getBody();   // Feign call
}

// Same signature + the exception. Called when the call fails
// or when the breaker is open (CallNotPermittedException).
private ProductOut priceFallback(String id, Throwable t) {
    throw new ResponseStatusException(
        HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE, "catalogue unavailable, try again later");
}

resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      product:
        sliding-window-size: 10                  # last 10 calls
        failure-rate-threshold: 50               # % → Open
        slow-call-duration-threshold: 2s         # slow = failure
        wait-duration-in-open-state: 30s         # Open → Half-Open
        permitted-number-of-calls-in-half-open-state: 3
  retry:
    instances:
      product:
        max-attempts: 3                          # 1 call + 2 retries
        wait-duration: 500ms
        enable-exponential-backoff: true         # 500 ms, 1 s, ...
        exponential-backoff-multiplier: 2

The breaker's state is exported as a metric (resilience4j_circuitbreaker_state) through Actuator, so you can graph it in Grafana (Hands-on 6).

The simulation below shows the circuit breaker cycling through all three states as the failure rate changes:

2026-10-13T23:43:55.522358 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

items.title: Fallback and graceful degradation
items.text:
Failing fast is better than hanging, but an error is still an error. A fallback is what the caller does instead when a call fails or the breaker is open. The goal is graceful degradation: lose a feature, not the whole page.

Dependency down Possible fallback in the store Recommendation service Show the "best sellers" list cached in Redis (Hands-on 8) Product service, for reads Serve the last cached product data, marked as possibly stale Notification service Publish the e-mail request to Kafka and send it later (Event-Driven Architecture) Payment service No safe fallback: answer 503 quickly with a clear message — never pretend the payment succeeded

A fallback must be safe and simple

A fallback that calls another remote service can fail too (and needs its own protection). And some operations — charging a card, reserving stock — must not be faked: failing clearly is the correct degraded behaviour.

items.title: Bulkhead
items.text:
The bulkhead pattern — named after watertight compartments in a ship hull — isolates resources by dependency. Rather than sharing a single thread pool across all downstream calls, each dependency gets its own pool.

flowchart TD
    gateway --> poolA["Thread Pool A\n(max 10 threads)"]
    gateway --> poolB["Thread Pool B\n(max 10 threads)"]
    poolA --> payment["Payment Service\n(degraded ⚠️)"]:::slow
    poolB --> inventory["Inventory Service\n(healthy ✓)"]:::ok

    classDef slow fill:#f90,color:#000
    classDef ok fill:#6c6,color:#fff

If Payment Service degrades and fills all 10 threads in Pool A, Pool B is completely unaffected. Inventory Service continues to handle requests at full speed. Without bulkheads, a single slow dependency saturates the shared pool and degrades all other calls equally.

The cost of bulkheads is resource overhead: ten separate pools of 10 threads each use more memory than one pool of 100 threads. The trade-off is almost always worth it for critical-path dependencies.

Resilience4j offers two kinds of bulkhead: a semaphore bulkhead (max-concurrent-calls, limits how many threads may be inside the call at once — cheap, the default) and a thread-pool bulkhead (the call runs in a dedicated pool). The same idea applies outside the JVM: separate database connection pools per workload, or separate Kubernetes deployments for critical and non-critical traffic.

items.title: Rate Limiting
items.text: Rate limiting caps the number of requests a client (or the system) can make within a time window, protecting services from traffic spikes and abusive clients.

items.title: Token bucket algorithm
items.text:
The token bucket is the most common rate limiting algorithm. It models a bucket that fills at a constant rate with tokens; each request consumes one token; requests that arrive when the bucket is empty are rejected or queued.

flowchart LR
    refill["Token source\n(refill rate: 100 req/s)"] -->|adds tokens| bucket["Token Bucket\n(capacity: 200)"]
    request["Incoming\nRequest"] -->|consumes 1 token| bucket
    bucket -->|tokens available| allowed["✓ Allowed"]
    bucket -->|bucket empty| rejected["✗ 429 Too Many Requests"]
Property Effect Refill rate Steady-state maximum throughput Bucket capacity (burst) How much instantaneous traffic above the rate is tolerated

A bucket capacity larger than the refill rate allows short bursts while still enforcing a long-term average. Spring Cloud Gateway's RequestRateLimiter filter (backed by Redis) and AWS API Gateway use a token bucket. Nginx limit_req uses the closely related leaky bucket: requests drain at a fixed rate and the burst parameter sets how many may wait in the queue.

Rate limiting at the store's edge (Nginx)

# 10 requests/s per client IP, bursts of up to 20 queued requests
limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=api:10m rate=10r/s;

server {
    location / {
        limit_req zone=api burst=20 nodelay;
        limit_req_status 429;
        proxy_pass http://gateway;
    }
}

This fits in front of the gateway replicas of Hands-on 7. Rate limits per user or per API key (rather than per IP) are usually applied in the gateway, where the authenticated identity is known.

items.title: Health Checks
items.text:
Health check endpoints allow orchestrators (Kubernetes, Docker Compose, load balancers) to detect failed instances and stop routing traffic to them before clients notice.

Two distinct types serve different purposes:

Liveness : Is the process alive? Returns 200 OK if the application is running and not deadlocked. If a liveness check fails, the orchestrator restarts the container.

Readiness : Is the service ready to serve traffic? Returns 200 OK only if the instance has finished starting and can do useful work (e.g. its own database is reachable). If a readiness check fails, the orchestrator removes the instance from the load balancer pool without restarting it.

Startup (Kubernetes) : Has the application finished starting? Liveness and readiness checks are not run until it succeeds, so a slow-starting JVM is not killed during boot.

flowchart LR
    lb["Load Balancer"] -->|"GET /actuator/health/readiness"| svc["Service Instance"]
    svc -->|200 OK| lb
    lb -->|routes traffic| svc

    svc2["Service Instance\n(db connection lost)"]
    lb -->|"GET /actuator/health/readiness"| svc2
    svc2 -->|503 DOWN| lb
    lb -->|removed from pool| svc2:::failed

    classDef failed fill:#f66,color:#fff

Spring Boot Actuator exposes both at /actuator/health/liveness and /actuator/health/readiness. They are enabled automatically when the application detects it runs on Kubernetes; elsewhere (e.g. Docker Compose) set management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true. By default they reflect only the application's internal state; add a dependency to readiness explicitly, e.g. management.endpoint.health.group.readiness.include=readinessState,db.

Probes for the order service on Kubernetes

# inside the container spec of the Deployment
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
  failureThreshold: 30        # up to 30 × 5 s = 150 s to start
  periodSeconds: 5
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 10
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 5

See Hands-on 5 for the Deployments these probes belong to.

Never put external dependencies in the liveness check

If liveness checks the database and the database blips, Kubernetes restarts every replica at the same time — turning a 10-second database hiccup into a full outage while all JVMs boot again. Liveness should answer only "is this process stuck?". Be careful even with readiness: if every replica depends on the same database, they all become unready together and the service disappears instead of returning clear errors.

items.title: Defence in depth
items.text:
These patterns are layered, not chosen in isolation. A production-grade call chain combines all of them:

flowchart LR
    client --> rl["Rate Limiter\n(protect service)"]
    rl --> cb["Circuit Breaker\n(fast-fail open deps)"]
    cb --> bh["Bulkhead\n(isolate thread pool)"]
    bh --> to["Timeout\n(bound wait time)"]
    to --> retry["Retry + Backoff\n(handle transients)"]
    retry --> downstream[Downstream Service]

Each layer handles a different failure scenario:

Layer What it handles Rate limiter Traffic spikes, abusive clients Circuit breaker Known-failing dependencies Bulkhead Slow dependencies bleeding into other calls Timeout Unbounded waiting Retry + backoff Transient errors

The order is a design decision

The diagram shows one common conceptual layering. Libraries make their own choice: in Resilience4j's Spring Boot integration the default aspect order is Retry ( CircuitBreaker ( RateLimiter ( TimeLimiter ( Bulkhead ( call ) ) ) ) ) — the retry is the outermost layer, so every attempt is counted by the circuit breaker and an open breaker makes the remaining attempts fail immediately. Whatever the order, check that retries do not bypass the breaker and that the sum of timeouts × attempts fits in the caller's own deadline.

items.title: Connections
items.text:
• Hands-on 1 — the Feign clients that need timeouts and breakers.
  • Hands-on 7 — Nginx in front of the gateway, where edge rate limiting lives.
  • Hands-on 9 — retries and dead letter queues for asynchronous consumers.
  • SLI / SLO / SLA — the budget these patterns protect.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Every remote call needs a timeout (connect + read), chosen per dependency and inside the caller's budget.
  • Retry only transient failures and idempotent operations, with exponential backoff and full jitter, at one layer only; use idempotency keys to make POST safe.
  • A circuit breaker (Closed → Open → Half-Open) fails fast on a dependency known to be down; pair it with a safe fallback.
  • Bulkheads keep one slow dependency from consuming all threads or connections; rate limiting (token / leaky bucket) protects the service from excess traffic.
  • Liveness restarts, readiness removes from the load balancer; never check external dependencies in liveness.
  • The patterns are layered; their order and combined timeouts must be designed, then verified with chaos experiments.

  1. NYGARD, M. Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. Pragmatic Programmers, 2018. ↩

  2. BROOKER, M. Exponential Backoff And Jitter. AWS Architecture Blog, 2015. ↩

  3. FOWLER, M. CircuitBreaker. martinfowler.com, 2014. ↩

  4. Resilience4j Documentation. ↩

items.title: SLI / SLO / SLA
items.text:
"Is the store reliable enough?" is a question nobody can answer without numbers. The product manager wants to ship a new checkout this week; the on-call engineer says the order service had a bad month and wants to freeze deploys. Without a shared definition of "good enough", that discussion is opinion against opinion. Measuring reliability requires a shared vocabulary that connects raw telemetry to engineering decisions to customer commitments. Google's Site Reliability Engineering practice introduced a three-tier model for this purpose1, now standard across the industry.

Term Full name Nature SLI Service Level Indicator A measurable metric SLO Service Level Objective An internal target for that metric SLA Service Level Agreement A contractual commitment to customers 
flowchart LR
    telemetry["Telemetry\n(logs, metrics, traces)"]
    sli["SLI\nRaw measurement"]
    slo["SLO\nInternal target"]
    sla["SLA\nExternal contract"]
    budget["Error Budget\nEngineering lever"]

    telemetry e1@-->|aggregated into| sli
    sli e2@-->|evaluated against| slo
    slo e3@-->|informs| sla
    slo e4@-->|remainder becomes| budget

    e1@{ animate: true }
    e2@{ animate: true }
    e3@{ animate: true }
    e4@{ animate: true }

items.title: SLI — The Raw Measurement
items.text:
An SLI is a quantitative metric pulled directly from instrumentation that reflects user-perceived system quality. Not every metric is a good SLI; only those that correlate with whether the user is getting value from the service.

The most useful way to write an SLI is as a ratio of events, so that it always lies between 0% and 100%2:

\[ \text{SLI} = \frac{\text{good events}}{\text{valid events}} \times 100\% \]

For example: "the proportion of GET /products requests that return a non-5xx status in less than 300 ms". "Valid" lets you exclude events that should not count, such as 4xx responses caused by the client.

items.title: Canonical SLI categories
items.text:
Category What it measures Example measurement Availability Fraction of requests served successfully non-5xx responses / total HTTP requests Latency Fraction of requests served fast enough requests faster than 200 ms / total requests (equivalently, P95 < 200 ms) Error rate Fraction of requests resulting in errors HTTP 5xx / total HTTP requests (the complement of availability) Throughput Volume of work the system processes Requests per second (usually a capacity metric rather than an SLI) Durability Fraction of data that can be retrieved Successful reads / total attempted reads Freshness Age of the most recent successful write Time since last successful cache refresh

Avoid vanity metrics

CPU utilisation, JVM heap size, and garbage collection pause time are not good SLIs on their own. A service can have 95% CPU and still serve all requests correctly — and conversely, a service can have 10% CPU and be completely down. SLIs must reflect what the user experiences, not what the infrastructure experiences.

items.title: How SLIs are collected
items.text:
• Application-level instrumentation: request counters and latency histograms exported via Spring Boot Actuator / Micrometer (Hands-on 6).
  • Synthetic monitoring: probes that send real requests from outside the system on a schedule (e.g. Prometheus Blackbox Exporter).
  • Log-based: parsing access logs to count 2xx vs 5xx responses.
  • Client-side: measuring from the browser or mobile client for true end-user experience.

The store's availability SLI in PromQL

Spring Boot exports the counter http_server_requests_seconds_count with a status label. The availability SLI of the order service over the last 5 minutes is:

sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{application="order", status!~"5.."}[5m]))
/
sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{application="order"}[5m]))

The numerator counts good events (anything that is not a 5xx), the denominator counts all events. See the Observability class for PromQL.

items.title: SLO — The Target You Commit To
items.text:
An SLO is a specific, time-bound target for an SLI. It answers: "How good does this metric need to be for us to consider the service healthy?"

Format:

SLI ≥ threshold over a rolling window

A rolling window always covers the last N days (for example, from 28 days ago until now), so it moves forward every minute; a calendar window resets on the 1st of each month.

Examples:

SLO Meaning Availability ≥ 99.9% over 28 days At most 0.1% of requests may fail in any 28-day period P95 latency ≤ 200 ms over 7 days 95% of requests complete within 200 ms in any 7-day window Error rate ≤ 0.5% over 24 hours No more than 5 in 1000 requests return 5xx in any day

items.title: Choosing the right SLO
items.text:
SLOs must be ambitious but achievable. An SLO that is never breached is not driving reliability work — it is too loose. An SLO that is constantly breached is noise — the team stops trusting it.

  • Start by measuring the current SLI over 30–90 days.
  • Set the initial SLO at the observed baseline minus a small buffer.
  • Tighten it over time as the system improves.
  • Make SLOs public within the engineering org so all teams understand the targets they are building toward.
  • Remember composite availability (overview): a service cannot promise more than the product of the services it synchronously depends on.

items.title: Error Budget
items.text:
The error budget is the quantity of unreliability the SLO permits. It is the engineering team's licence to take risk.

\[ \text{Error Budget} = 1 - \text{SLO target} \]

For a 99.9% availability SLO, the budget is 0.1% — of the time or of the requests in the window, depending on how the SLI is defined.

Time-basedRequest-based

For a 99.9% SLO over a 28-day window:

\[ \text{Error Budget} = 0.1\% \times 28 \text{ days} \times 24 \text{ h} \times 60 \text{ min} \approx 40.3 \text{ minutes} \]

(Over a 30.44-day calendar month the same 99.9% gives ≈ 43.8 minutes — the number usually quoted in "nines" tables.)

The order service receives about 1,000,000 requests per day. Over 28 days that is 28,000,000 requests, so a 99.9% SLO allows

\[ 0.1\% \times 28\,000\,000 = 28\,000 \text{ failed requests} \]

A bad deploy that returns 500 for 20,000 requests in an hour consumes about 70% of the month's budget at once.

If the error budget is intact, the team can:

  • Deploy frequently and accept some deployment risk
  • Run experiments on production systems
  • Take on more technical debt

If the error budget is exhausted, the team must:

  • Freeze non-essential deployments
  • Prioritise reliability work over feature work
  • Investigate and fix the root causes consuming the budget

These rules only work if they are agreed in advance: an error budget policy is a short document, signed by product and engineering, that says what happens when the budget runs out.

Error budget as a negotiation tool

When a product manager wants to ship a risky feature and the SRE team is reluctant, the error budget provides an objective answer: "We have 12 minutes of budget remaining in this 28-day window. If we deploy and it causes 30 minutes of degradation, we will miss our SLO. Let's wait until enough budget has been recovered."

items.title: Burn rate
items.text:
Burn rate measures how fast the error budget is being consumed relative to the SLO window2:

\[ \text{burn rate} = \frac{\text{observed error rate}}{1 - \text{SLO}} \]

With a 99.9% SLO, an error rate of 0.1% is a burn rate of 1 — the budget lasts exactly the whole window. An error rate of 1.44% is a burn rate of 14.4. A burn rate of \(b\) exhausts the budget in (window ÷ \(b\)).

For a 28-day window:

Burn rate Budget exhausted in Severity 1× End of SLO window (28 days) Normal 2× 14 days Warning 6× ~4.7 days High — open a ticket 14.4× ~1.9 days (~47 hours) Critical — page immediately

The thresholds 14.4× and 6× come from the SRE Workbook: sustained for 1 hour, a 14.4× burn consumes about 2% of the budget; sustained for 6 hours, a 6× burn consumes about 5%. (The Workbook derives them for a 30-day window; with 28 days the percentages are almost the same.) High burn-rate alerts catch fast-moving incidents early, while low burn-rate alerts catch slow degradation that would otherwise be invisible2.

A burn-rate alert for the order service

# Prometheus alerting rule (99.9% SLO → budget = 0.001)
- alert: OrderErrorBudgetFastBurn
  expr: |
    (
      sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{application="order", status=~"5.."}[1h]))
      /
      sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{application="order"}[1h]))
    ) > (14.4 * 0.001)
  for: 2m
  labels:
    severity: page

The alert fires on a symptom users feel (errors burning the budget), not on a cause such as CPU — see alerting in the Observability class.

items.title: SLA — The Contractual Commitment
items.text: An SLA is a formal agreement between service provider and customer that defines the expected level of service and the remedies (typically service credits) if that level is not met. SLAs are legal documents; missing them has financial consequences.

items.title: Structure of an SLA
items.text:
1. Covered services — which products and regions are in scope
  2. SLO targets — the availability or latency commitments
  3. Measurement methodology — how uptime is calculated, which incidents count
  4. Exclusions — scheduled maintenance, force majeure, customer-caused outages
  5. Remedies — service credit schedule for each tier of breach

items.title: Real-world SLA examples
items.text:
The commitments below are taken from the providers' public SLA pages34; the exact conditions (deployment type, region, credit tiers) change over time, so always read the current page.

Provider Service Committed monthly uptime Remedy for breach AWS EC2 (region level) 99.99% Tiered service credits AWS S3 Standard 99.9% Tiered service credits AWS RDS Multi-AZ 99.95% Tiered service credits Google Cloud Compute Engine (instances in multiple zones) 99.99% Tiered service credits Azure Virtual Machines (across Availability Zones) 99.99% Tiered service credits

Notice two things. First, the higher numbers apply only when you deploy redundantly (multiple zones, Multi-AZ) — redundancy is the price of the extra nine. Second, the remedy is a credit on your bill, not compensation for your lost sales: an SLA transfers some financial risk, it does not make your system available.

items.title: SLA vs SLO
items.text:
SLA and SLO are often confused. The critical distinction:

SLO SLA Audience Engineering team Customer / business Nature Internal target Legal contract Strictness Higher (stricter) Lower (more lenient) Consequence of breach Reliability work, feature freeze Service credits, penalties

Best practice: set your SLO stricter than your SLA. The buffer between SLO and SLA is the safety margin that prevents a reliability incident from triggering contractual penalties. If the SLA is 99.9%, the SLO might be 99.95%.

items.title: Best practices
items.text:
Practice Rationale Fewer, more meaningful SLIs Two or three well-chosen indicators outperform ten noisy ones. Start with availability and P99 latency. 28-day rolling windows Four weeks always contain the same number of weekdays and weekend days, so the SLI is not distorted by calendar months of different lengths. Automate SLO dashboards Manual calculation is error-prone and too slow. Grafana + Prometheus or Cloud Monitoring should show current SLO compliance in real time. Review SLOs quarterly User expectations and system capabilities evolve. SLOs that were correct at launch may need adjustment after a year of scale. Never set SLO = 100% 100% is unachievable and leaves no room for planned maintenance or safe deployments.

Common pitfalls

  • Measuring the wrong thing: an SLI computed only from the health-check endpoint says nothing about POST /orders.
  • Averages instead of percentiles: a mean latency of 80 ms can hide 5% of users waiting 4 s. Use percentiles or "fraction of requests faster than X".
  • Mixing windows: an error budget computed over 30 days compared with an SLO over 28 days gives wrong decisions.
  • SLO without a policy: if nothing changes when the budget is gone, the SLO is just a number on a dashboard.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• An SLI is a ratio of good events to valid events that reflects what users feel; an SLO is a target for it over a window; an SLA is a contract with penalties, looser than the SLO.
  • The error budget is 1 − SLO, in time or in requests: 99.9% over 28 days ≈ 40.3 minutes (≈ 43.8 minutes over a 30.44-day month).
  • Burn rate = observed error rate ÷ budget; 14.4× empties a 28-day budget in about 2 days and should page someone.
  • The budget turns "ship or freeze?" into a data-driven decision — if there is an agreed policy.
  • Always state the window and use percentiles, never averages, for latency.

  1. BEYER, B. et al. Site Reliability Engineering. Google / O'Reilly, 2016. Chapters 3–4 (Embracing Risk; Service Level Objectives). ↩

  2. BEYER, B. et al. The Site Reliability Workbook. Google / O'Reilly, 2018. Chapter 2 — Implementing SLOs; Chapter 5 — Alerting on SLOs. ↩↩↩

  3. AWS Service Level Agreements. Amazon Web Services. ↩

  4. Google Cloud Service Level Agreements. Google LLC. ↩

items.title: Security: OAuth 2.0, OIDC & Zero Trust
items.text:
In Hands-on 3 we secured the store with a homemade scheme: auth-service checks the password, signs a JSON Web Token (JWT) with an HMAC secret and returns it in a cookie; on every request the gateway asks auth-service to resolve the token and forwards the caller's id in the id-account header. That works for one web app with one login form. Now the store wants "Sign in with Google", a mobile app, a nightly job that calls order-service with no user behind it, and — one day — a vulnerable library lets an attacker run code inside the product-service pod. The homemade scheme has no answer to any of these.

JWT is a transport format — it carries claims such as "this is account 42". It says nothing about how the user proved their identity, who may issue tokens, how a third-party app gets access without seeing the password, or why one service should trust a call from another. OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect are the standards that fill these gaps; Zero Trust is the architecture that stops trusting the network itself: distrust everything, verify always.

Learning objectives

By the end of this class you should be able to:

  • Distinguish authentication from authorization and point out which component of the store performs each one.
  • Explain the four OAuth 2.0 roles and choose the right grant (Authorization Code + PKCE, Client Credentials, Device Code) for a given client.
  • Compare access, refresh and ID tokens, and explain what OpenID Connect adds on top of OAuth 2.0.
  • Configure a gateway to validate JWTs locally with a JWKS, and compare it with the remote validation (/auth/solve) used in Hands-on 3.
  • Apply Zero Trust controls — mTLS, NetworkPolicy, least privilege — to service-to-service traffic in Kubernetes.
  • Choose a secrets-management approach and explain why a base64 Kubernetes Secret is not encryption.

Prerequisite

This class builds on the JWT concepts from Hands-on 3. Make sure you are comfortable with the JWT structure (header.payload.signature), the sub, exp and iss claims, and how the gateway validates tokens before reading this — see Hands-on 3 — JWT and Hands-on 3 — Authorization.

items.title: Slides
items.text: Click the slides and use ← → to move through them; F goes full screen and P opens the presenter view, with the notes. Open the slides in a new tab

items.title: Roadmap
items.text:
1. Overview (this page) — authentication vs. authorization, what Hands-on 3 built, what JWT alone cannot do, and the map of security layers of the store.
  2. OAuth 2.0 & OpenID Connect — roles, tokens and scopes, grant types (Authorization Code + PKCE, Client Credentials), OIDC and the ID Token, and how the gateway validates tokens (JWKS vs. introspection).
  3. Zero Trust, mTLS & Secrets — perimeter vs. Zero Trust, mutual TLS and workload identity, Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, and secrets management.

items.title: Authentication vs. authorization
items.text:
Two questions are asked on every request, and they are often confused:

Authentication (authN) Authorization (authZ) Question Who are you? What are you allowed to do? Input a credential: password, certificate, token the authenticated identity + a policy (roles, scopes, ownership) Failure 401 Unauthorized (no or invalid credential) 403 Forbidden (valid identity, not allowed) In the store auth-service checks email + password at POST /auth/login; the gateway checks the token on each request order-service checks that order 123 belongs to the id-account that asked for it

A few terms used throughout the class:

  • Principal — the authenticated entity: a user (ada@store.com) or a workload (order-service).
  • Credential — what a principal presents to prove its identity (a password, a private key, a token).
  • Token — a string issued after authentication that the principal presents instead of the credential. A bearer token grants access to whoever holds it, like cash: steal it and you can spend it.
  • Claim — a statement inside a token, such as "sub": "42" or "scope": "orders:read".

Authorization is not done once at the gateway

The gateway can say "this is account 42". Only order-service knows whether order 123 belongs to account 42. Forgetting this check — GET /orders/123 returns any order to any logged-in user — is Broken Object Level Authorization, the number-one risk in the OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023)1.

items.title: What Hands-on 3 built
items.text:
The flow below is the one you implemented: the token is a reference that only auth-service can read, and the gateway asks for it on every call.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor B as Browser
    participant GW as gateway-service
    participant AU as auth-service
    participant AC as account-service
    B->>GW: POST /auth/login {email, password}
    GW->>AU: forward (open route)
    AU->>AU: check password, sign JWT (HMAC secret)
    AU-->>B: Set-Cookie: __store_jwt_token
    B->>GW: GET /accounts/me + cookie
    GW->>AU: POST /auth/solve {token}
    AU-->>GW: {idAccount}
    GW->>AC: GET /accounts/me + id-account header
    AC-->>B: 200 OK

It is a sound design for a single application, and it has three properties worth naming:

  • Symmetric signature (HMAC, e.g. HS256) — the same secret signs and verifies. Only auth-service holds JWT_SECRET_KEY, so only it can validate tokens; that is why the gateway must call it.
  • Remote validation — one extra network hop per request, but auth-service could refuse a token immediately (for example, after logout).
  • Trust in the network — account-service believes any id-account header, because only the gateway can reach it inside the Docker network.

items.title: What JWT alone cannot do
items.text: Problem Homemade JWT (Hands-on 3) Standard answer Where Third-party login ("Sign in with Google") ✗ no way to delegate Authorization Code + PKCE flow OAuth Service-to-service calls with no user ✗ no standard; services reuse a user token or a shared password Client Credentials grant OAuth Let other services verify tokens themselves ✗ HMAC secret would have to be copied to every service asymmetric keys published as a JWKS OAuth Revoke a token before it expires only with a remote check on every call short-lived access tokens + refresh tokens; introspection OAuth Standard user identity for the client app ✗ ad-hoc claims OIDC ID Token + UserInfo endpoint OAuth A compromised pod calling other services ✗ the internal network is trusted mTLS, NetworkPolicy, authorization policies Zero Trust

items.title: The security layers of the store
items.text:
No single control protects a system. Defense in depth stacks independent layers, so that an attacker who defeats one still faces the next. The diagram follows a request from the Internet down to the data:

flowchart LR
    U(["Client"]) -->|"HTTPS (TLS)"| GW["Gateway<br>validates token"]
    IdP["Identity Provider<br>(auth-service / Keycloak)"] -->|"issues tokens"| U
    GW -->|"identity header<br>(mTLS inside)"| SVC["order-service<br>checks ownership"]
    SVC -->|"allowed by<br>NetworkPolicy"| PS["product-service"]
    SVC -->|"short-lived<br>DB credential"| DB[("Postgres")]
Layer Threat Control Where in the course Edge eavesdropping, abuse TLS, rate limiting Hands-on 2 — Gateway, Hands-on 7 — Nginx Identity stolen or forged credentials OAuth 2.0 / OIDC, short-lived tokens OAuth 2.0 & OIDC, Hands-on 3 Request user reads someone else's data authorization in each service (ownership, roles, scopes) this page Service-to-service lateral movement from a compromised pod mTLS, NetworkPolicy, authorization policies Zero Trust, Hands-on 5 Data leaked passwords and keys secrets manager, encryption at rest Zero Trust — Secrets

Common mistakes

  • Security only at the gateway. If any service is reachable without passing through the gateway (a NodePort, a debug port, a misconfigured Ingress), anyone can send id-account: <any id> and impersonate any user.
  • Rolling your own crypto or protocol. Hashing, signing and token flows are subtle; use a vetted library (JJWT, Spring Security) and a standard flow.
  • Long-lived bearer tokens. Hands-on 3 issues 24-hour tokens; a stolen one is valid for a day. Short access tokens plus refresh tokens shrink that window.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Authentication answers who, authorization answers what; the gateway authenticates, but each service must still authorize access to its own objects.
  • A JWT is only a format. OAuth 2.0 defines how tokens are obtained and delegated; OIDC adds a standard identity (ID Token).
  • Hands-on 3 uses a symmetric key and remote validation; standard deployments use asymmetric keys and a JWKS so any service can validate locally.
  • Zero Trust removes the assumption that the internal network is safe: every call carries a verifiable identity and is checked against a policy.
  • Security is layered: TLS at the edge, tokens for users, mTLS and NetworkPolicy between services, a secrets manager for credentials.

  1. OWASP. API1:2023 — Broken Object Level Authorization. OWASP API Security Top 10, 2023. ↩

items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: Fundamentals
items.text:
Q1. A logged-in customer calls GET /orders/123 and receives an order that belongs to another customer. The gateway validated the token correctly. What is missing?

  • A. Authentication — the gateway should have returned 401 Unauthorized
  • B. Authorization at the object level — order-service must check that order 123 belongs to the caller's id-account
  • C. TLS — the response was read by someone in the middle
  • D. A longer token expiry
Answer

B — Object-level authorization in order-service.

The caller is authenticated: the token is valid, so 401 would be wrong. The failure is authorization: only order-service knows who owns order 123, so it must compare the owner with the identity the gateway forwarded and answer 403 Forbidden (or 404) otherwise. This is Broken Object Level Authorization, the first item of the OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023).

items.title: OAuth 2.0 & OIDC
items.text:
Q2. In OAuth 2.0, which role issues access tokens?

  • A. Resource Owner
  • B. Client
  • C. Authorization Server
  • D. Resource Server
Answer

C — Authorization Server.

The Authorization Server authenticates the user, obtains their consent, and issues tokens. The Resource Server validates tokens but never creates them. The Client requests tokens on behalf of the Resource Owner.

Q3. Why is PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) required for public clients (mobile/SPA apps)?

  • A. It encrypts the access token in transit
  • B. It prevents authorization code interception attacks — the code alone is useless without the code_verifier that only the legitimate client possesses
  • C. It replaces the client_secret for confidential clients
  • D. It extends the access token lifetime
Answer

B — It prevents authorization code interception attacks.

Public clients cannot securely store a client_secret. PKCE generates a random code_verifier, hashes it to a code_challenge (SHA-256, base64url), and sends the challenge with the authorization request. Only the original client can complete the token exchange because only it knows the verifier. PKCE does not replace the secret of a confidential client — current best practice (RFC 9700) recommends PKCE for confidential clients as well.

Q4. What claim in an OIDC ID Token proves which application the token was issued for?

Answer

aud (audience) — must contain the client_id of the receiving application. If a token's aud does not match, the client must reject it to prevent token substitution attacks where a token issued for one app is replayed against another. Resource servers apply the same rule to access tokens: reject any token whose aud is not their own API.

Q5. The store's mobile app holds an access token with exp 5 minutes from now. What should the app do when it expires?

Answer

Use the refresh_token to request a new access_token from the Authorization Server. The app should not ask the user to log in again just because an access token expired — that is what refresh tokens are for. The refresh token is long-lived, stored securely by the client, and sent only to the Authorization Server. Only when the refresh token itself is expired or revoked must the user log in again. (A resource server that receives the expired token simply answers 401; it does not refresh anything.)

Q6. What is the JWKS endpoint used for?

Answer

It publishes the Authorization Server's public signing keys so Resource Servers and the Gateway can validate JWT signatures locally, without calling the auth server on every request. Each key has a kid, and each JWT header names the kid that signed it. Key rotation is handled by updating the JWKS — services re-fetch on an unknown kid, so they always use current keys without redeployment.

Q7. What is the key difference between an ID Token and an Access Token?

Answer

ID Token = who the user is (identity). Access Token = what the client is allowed to do (authorization). The ID Token is consumed by the Client to learn about the user and establish a session; its audience is the client. The Access Token is sent to Resource Servers to authorize API calls; the client should treat it as opaque and never parse it. APIs must not accept ID tokens.

Q8. A microservice needs to call another microservice with no user involved (background job). Which OAuth 2.0 grant type should it use?

Answer

Client Credentials grant. The calling service authenticates with its own credentials (client_id and client_secret, or a signed assertion) to obtain an access token scoped to what it needs, such as stock:read. No user context is involved, making it the correct choice for machine-to-machine communication such as background jobs, scheduled tasks, or inter-service data pipelines.

Q9. In Hands-on 3, the gateway calls POST /auth/solve on every request. A colleague proposes switching to RS256 tokens validated locally at the gateway with a JWKS. Which statement about this change is correct?

  • A. Local validation is always strictly better — there is no tradeoff
  • B. Local validation removes a network hop and keeps working if auth-service is down, but a token can no longer be rejected before its exp
  • C. Local validation requires copying the HMAC secret to the gateway
  • D. Local validation makes logout immediate
Answer

B — Faster and more available, but revocation waits for exp.

With asymmetric keys the gateway only needs the public key from the JWKS, so no secret is copied (C is wrong) and no call is made per request. The price is revocation: a self-contained JWT stays valid until it expires, so logout is not immediate (D is wrong). That is why locally validated access tokens are kept short-lived and paired with refresh tokens; /auth/solve is a form of token introspection, which gives immediate revocation at the cost of a hop per request.

items.title: Zero Trust & Secrets
items.text:
Q10. In mTLS, what does the client present that it does NOT present in standard TLS?

Answer

Its own X.509 certificate (and a proof that it holds the matching private key). In standard TLS only the server is authenticated to the client. In mTLS both server and client present certificates, so each side knows the other's identity — for example the SPIFFE ID spiffe://cluster.local/ns/store/sa/order-service. mTLS only proves who is calling; an authorization policy still decides whether that caller may call.

Q11. What does "never trust, always verify" mean in the context of Zero Trust, specifically for internal service calls?

Answer

Even a call from service A to service B within the same Kubernetes cluster must present a valid identity credential and be authorised against a policy. Internal network location does not grant trust — every request is treated as potentially hostile. This prevents lateral movement after a breach, where an attacker who has compromised one service cannot freely reach others.

Q12. You apply a NetworkPolicy that allows only gateway-service to reach order-service, on a default minikube cluster. From another pod, curl order-service:8080 still works. What is the most likely cause?

  • A. NetworkPolicies only apply to egress traffic
  • B. The cluster's network (CNI) plugin does not enforce NetworkPolicy, so the object is accepted but ignored
  • C. NetworkPolicies take 24 hours to propagate
  • D. Port 8080 is always open in Kubernetes
Answer

B — The CNI plugin does not enforce NetworkPolicy.

The Kubernetes API stores NetworkPolicy objects on any cluster, but enforcement is done by the network plugin. Calico and Cilium enforce policies; the default minikube network does not. Start minikube with --cni=calico to see the policy take effect.

Q13. Why are Kubernetes Secrets NOT considered secure by default?

Answer

Secrets are stored as base64-encoded strings in etcd, and base64 is not encryption — it can be trivially decoded (echo c3RvcmU= | base64 -d prints store). Without etcd encryption at rest and strict RBAC on Secrets, any principal allowed to read Secrets — or to create a pod that mounts them — can read them in plain text. Production systems enable encryption at rest, keep secret manifests out of Git, and often use an external secrets manager such as HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager.

Q14. What is the main security benefit of Vault dynamic secrets for order-service's database access?

  • A. The database password is longer
  • B. Each requester gets a unique, short-lived credential that Vault revokes when its lease expires, so a stolen credential stops working by itself and every use is attributable
  • C. The password is stored in a ConfigMap instead of a Secret
  • D. The database no longer needs authentication
Answer

B — Unique, short-lived, automatically revoked credentials.

With a static password shared by every replica, a leak is valid until someone notices and rotates it — and rotating breaks everyone. With dynamic secrets, Vault creates a database user per lease (for example, one hour) and drops it at expiry; the audit log shows which workload used which credential.

items.title: OAuth 2.0 & OpenID Connect
items.text: The store launches a mobile app and wants a "Sign in with Google" button. The app must never see the user's Google password, Google must know which app is asking, and the user must be able to say "this app may read my email address, nothing else". At the same time, a nightly job in order-service needs to call product-service to reconcile stock — and there is no user at all. A homemade login endpoint cannot express any of this. OAuth 2.01 is the standard framework for delegated authorization, and OpenID Connect5 is the identity layer built on top of it.

items.title: OAuth 2.0 in one sentence
items.text: OAuth 2.0 lets a client application obtain a limited, revocable access token to call an API on behalf of a user — or on its own behalf — without ever handling the user's password. The user authenticates only at the Authorization Server, and consents to the access requested.

items.title: Roles
items.text:
Role Description In the store Resource Owner The user who owns the data Ada, a customer Client The application requesting access the store's web frontend, the mobile app, a nightly job Authorization Server Authenticates the user and issues tokens Keycloak, Auth0, AWS Cognito — or our auth-service Resource Server API that holds the protected resource and validates tokens order-service, account-service (behind the gateway)

Clients come in two kinds, and the difference drives the choice of flow:

  • Confidential client — runs on a server and can keep a secret (client_secret) safe: a backend, a batch job.
  • Public client — runs on the user's device and cannot keep a secret: a single-page app (anyone can read its JavaScript), a mobile app (anyone can decompile it).

items.title: Tokens
items.text:
Token Purpose Audience Typical lifetime Access token authorizes API calls; sent as Authorization: Bearer <token>3 the Resource Server 5–60 minutes Refresh token obtains a new access token without a new login the Authorization Server only hours to weeks ID token (OIDC) tells the client who the user is the Client only minutes

An access token can be self-contained (a JWT the resource server verifies by itself) or opaque (a random reference string the resource server must look up at the Authorization Server). The Hands-on 3 token is a JWT, but the gateway treats it as opaque: it asks auth-service to resolve it.

items.title: Scopes and claims
items.text:
A scope is a named permission the client asks for and the user consents to, such as openid, email or orders:read. The granted scopes travel in the access token's scope claim. The Resource Server then combines what the client may do (scopes) with who the user is and what they may do (sub, roles) and which object is being accessed (ownership).

Checking a scope in Spring Security

Spring Security turns each scope in a JWT into an authority prefixed with SCOPE_, so an endpoint can require it declaratively:

@GetMapping("/orders")
@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_orders:read')")
public List<OrderOut> findMine(@AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) {
    return orderService.findByAccount(jwt.getSubject()); // ownership: only this user's orders
}

items.title: Grant types
items.text:
A grant (or flow) is the procedure a client follows to obtain a token. Choosing the grant is the first design decision.

Grant Use case Status Authorization Code + PKCE web, SPA and mobile apps where a user logs in recommended default for every user-facing client Client Credentials service-to-service, no user involved recommended for machine-to-machine Device Authorization4 devices without a browser or keyboard (smart TV, CLI) recommended for that niche Refresh Token exchange a refresh token for a new access token used together with the flows above Implicit old SPAs: token returned directly in the URL deprecated — tokens leak via URL and history Resource Owner Password (ROPC) legacy: the client collects the password must not be used2 
flowchart TD
    q1{"Is a user<br>involved?"} -->|no| cc["Client Credentials"]
    q1 -->|yes| q2{"Does the device<br>have a browser?"}
    q2 -->|yes| pkce["Authorization Code + PKCE"]
    q2 -->|no| dev["Device Authorization"]

Never use ROPC

Resource Owner Password Credentials requires the client to collect the user's username and password directly. This defeats the purpose of OAuth 2.0 (delegated authorization without sharing credentials), cannot support multi-factor login, and teaches users to type passwords into any app. The OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice (RFC 9700) says it must not be used, and the OAuth 2.1 draft removes it together with the Implicit grant2.

items.title: Authorization Code + PKCE
items.text:
The user logs in at the Authorization Server, never in the app. The app receives a short-lived, single-use authorization code through a browser redirect and exchanges it for tokens in a direct back-channel call. PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange, pronounced "pixy")6 binds the code to the app that started the flow:

  1. The app creates a random code_verifier (43–128 characters) and keeps it in memory.
  2. It sends only its hash, code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA-256(code_verifier)), in the authorization request.
  3. When exchanging the code, it sends the original code_verifier; the server hashes it and compares.

An attacker who intercepts the redirect (a malicious app registered for the same URL scheme, a leaked log) gets the code but not the verifier, so the code is useless.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor User
    participant App as Client App
    participant Auth as Authorization Server (Keycloak)
    participant API as Resource Server (order-service)

    User->>App: click "Login"
    App->>App: generate state, code_verifier, code_challenge (S256)
    App->>Auth: redirect to /authorize?response_type=code&client_id&code_challenge&state
    Auth->>User: login form (and consent)
    User->>Auth: credentials (+ MFA)
    Auth->>App: redirect to callback ?code=AUTH_CODE&state
    App->>App: check state matches
    App->>Auth: POST /token {code, code_verifier}
    Auth->>App: {access_token, refresh_token, id_token}
    App->>API: GET /orders  Authorization: Bearer access_token
    API->>API: verify signature with cached JWKS, check exp, iss, aud, scope
    API->>App: 200 OK order data

The state parameter is a random value the app checks on the way back; it prevents an attacker from injecting their own code into the victim's session (a CSRF attack on the callback).

Computing a PKCE pair by hand 
# 64 random URL-safe characters
verifier=$(openssl rand -base64 48 | tr -d '=+/\n' | cut -c1-64)
# BASE64URL(SHA-256(verifier)), without '=' padding
challenge=$(printf '%s' "$verifier" | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary \
            | openssl base64 | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '=')
echo "verifier=$verifier"; echo "challenge=$challenge"

items.title: Client Credentials
items.text:
When no user is involved, the client authenticates as itself with its own credentials and receives a token that represents the service, not a person.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Job as order-service (nightly job)
    participant Auth as Authorization Server (Keycloak)
    participant P as product-service
    Job->>Auth: POST /token grant_type=client_credentials, client_id, client_secret
    Auth-->>Job: access_token (sub=order-service, scope=stock:read)
    Job->>P: GET /products/stock  Bearer access_token
    P->>P: verify token, check scope stock:read
    P-->>Job: 200 OK
curl -s -X POST http://keycloak:8080/realms/store/protocol/openid-connect/token \
  -d grant_type=client_credentials \
  -d client_id=order-service \
  -d client_secret="$ORDER_SERVICE_SECRET" \
  -d scope=stock:read

Do not reuse a user's token for background work

A job that borrows "some user's" token breaks the audit trail (who did this?), stops working when that token expires, and usually has far more permissions than it needs. Give each service its own client and only the scopes it needs.

items.title: Token lifecycle
items.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Active : issued by POST /token
    Active --> Expired : exp reached
    Active --> Revoked : logout / admin action
    Expired --> Active : client presents refresh_token, gets a new access token
    Expired --> [*] : refresh token also expired, user logs in again
    Revoked --> [*]

The access token is short-lived (typically 5–60 minutes) and sent with every API request. The refresh token is long-lived (hours to weeks), stored securely by the client, and sent only to the Authorization Server to obtain new access tokens without prompting the user again. For public clients, the server should use refresh token rotation: each use returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one, so a stolen refresh token is detected the moment both the thief and the legitimate app try to use it2.

Why short access tokens? A self-contained JWT cannot be "un-issued": a resource server that validates it locally will accept it until exp. Keeping exp short bounds the damage of a stolen token, while revocation is enforced where the refresh token is exchanged.

items.title: OpenID Connect (OIDC)
items.text:
OAuth 2.0 handles authorization ("can this client access this resource?"). It deliberately does not say who the user is — an access token is meant for the API, not for the client to read. OpenID Connect adds authentication ("who is this user?") by defining an ID Token — a JWT with standardised user claims, addressed to the client5.

OIDC extends OAuth 2.0 with three additions:

  • The openid scope in the authorization request
  • ID Token — a JWT containing user identity claims (sub, name, email, iss, aud)
  • UserInfo endpoint — GET /userinfo returns additional profile claims on demand

items.title: ID Token claims
items.text:
Claim Meaning sub Subject — unique, stable user identifier at this provider iss Issuer — URL of the authorization server aud Audience — must contain the client's client_id exp / iat Expiry / issued-at timestamps name, email Standard user profile claims (requested with the profile and email scopes) nonce Value sent by the client in the request and echoed back — prevents replaying an old ID token

The client must validate the ID token before trusting it: signature, iss, aud equal to its own client_id, exp, and nonce.

items.title: OAuth 2.0 and OIDC layers
items.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph oidc ["OIDC layer (identity)"]
        id["ID Token<br>(who is the user?)"]
        ui["UserInfo endpoint"]
    end
    subgraph oauth ["OAuth 2.0 layer (authorization)"]
        at["Access Token<br>(what can the client do?)"]
        rt["Refresh Token"]
    end
    app["Client App"] --> id
    app --> at
    at -->|"sent to"| api["Resource Server"]

The Authorization Server exposes a discovery document at GET /.well-known/openid-configuration which returns all endpoint URLs (authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint, userinfo_endpoint), supported scopes, and the jwks_uri. Clients and resource servers can bootstrap from the issuer URL alone, without hardcoded configuration.

items.title: Common OIDC providers
items.text:
Provider Use case Keycloak Self-hosted, open source, full-featured — ideal for internal services and for the course Auth0 Managed cloud, fast integration AWS Cognito Native AWS integration Google / GitHub Social login for public-facing apps

Do not call APIs with the ID token

The ID token's audience is the client, not your API. Resource servers must accept access tokens only, and must reject tokens whose aud is not their own — otherwise a token issued for another app can be replayed against yours.

items.title: Validating tokens at the gateway
items.text: Rather than every microservice implementing validation, the gateway is the first enforcement point: it rejects requests without a valid token and forwards a trusted identity downstream. There are two ways to validate.

items.title: Local validation with JWKS
items.text:
With asymmetric signatures (RS256, ES256) the Authorization Server signs with a private key that never leaves it, and anyone can verify with the matching public key. The public keys are published as a JSON Web Key Set (JWKS)7 — a JSON document where each key has a kid (key id); every JWT header names the kid that signed it.

  1. The Authorization Server publishes its public keys at its jwks_uri (Keycloak: /realms/<realm>/protocol/openid-connect/certs).
  2. The gateway fetches and caches the JWKS.
  3. Each incoming request carries Authorization: Bearer <token>.
  4. The gateway picks the key by kid and verifies the signature locally — no call to the Authorization Server.
  5. On an unknown kid (the server rotated its keys): re-fetch the JWKS once, then retry.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant GW as API Gateway
    participant Auth as Auth Server
    participant SVC as order-service

    GW->>Auth: GET jwks_uri (at startup, then cached)
    Auth-->>GW: {keys: [{kid, kty, n, e}]}
    C->>GW: GET /orders  Bearer token
    GW->>GW: verify signature with cached key, check exp, iss, aud
    alt token invalid
        GW-->>C: 401 Unauthorized
    else token valid
        GW->>SVC: GET /orders + id-account header
        SVC-->>GW: 200 OK
        GW-->>C: 200 OK
    end

With Spring Security (also in the reactive Spring Cloud Gateway), local validation is configuration only:

application.yml (issuer)application.yml (JWKS only) 
spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          # discovers jwks_uri and also validates the iss claim
          issuer-uri: http://keycloak:8080/realms/store
          # Spring Boot 3.1+: also reject tokens whose aud is not this API
          audiences: store-api

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          jwk-set-uri: http://keycloak:8080/realms/store/protocol/openid-connect/certs

Whatever the library, a correct validation checks8:

  • the signature, with an algorithm from an explicit allow-list — never alg: none, and never let the token header choose the algorithm;
  • exp and nbf (with a small clock skew);
  • iss — the token comes from your Authorization Server;
  • aud — the token was issued for this API;
  • the scopes / roles required by the endpoint.

items.title: Remote validation (introspection)
items.text:
The alternative is to ask the Authorization Server on every request: "is this token valid, and whose is it?". OAuth standardises this as token introspection (RFC 7662)9. The POST /auth/solve call in Hands-on 3 — Authorization is exactly this pattern, with a custom endpoint.

Local (JWKS) Remote (introspection, /auth/solve) Latency no extra hop one network call per request (cacheable) Availability works while the Auth Server is down Auth Server outage = every request fails Revocation effective only at exp immediate Key handling public keys only; private key stays in one place any key type; the secret stays in the Auth Server Token type JWT JWT or opaque

Large systems often combine both: short-lived JWTs validated locally for most calls, introspection for sensitive operations.

Forward user context downstream

After validation, the gateway forwards the identity as a header — id-account: <sub> in Hands-on 3 — so downstream services do not need to parse tokens. Downstream services must only accept this header from the gateway: strip it from incoming external requests, and make sure services are not reachable from outside (see Zero Trust). Some teams forward the original token instead (token relay), so each service can verify it again.

items.title: Where the browser keeps the token
items.text:
Storage Readable by JavaScript? Main risk Mitigation localStorage / sessionStorage yes any XSS script steals the token avoid for tokens HttpOnly cookie (Hands-on 3) no CSRF — the browser sends the cookie automatically SameSite, Secure, CSRF tokens Server-side session (Backend for Frontend) no token in the browser at all session theft the BFF holds tokens; the browser holds only a session cookie

Hands-on 3 chose the HttpOnly cookie: see the cookie flags in Hands-on 3 — Open Routes.

items.title: Pitfalls
items.text:
Common mistakes with OAuth 2.0 and JWT

  • Using ROPC or Implicit in new code — use Authorization Code + PKCE.
  • Skipping the aud check — a valid token for another API is accepted by yours.
  • Long-lived access tokens — a stolen bearer token is valid until exp; keep them short and use refresh tokens.
  • Sharing an HMAC secret among many services — every service that can verify can also forge tokens; use asymmetric keys and a JWKS.
  • Tokens in URLs or logs — query strings end up in proxy logs and browser history; send tokens in headers or cookies, and mask them in logs.
  • Calling the API with the ID token — ID tokens are for the client; APIs accept access tokens.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• OAuth 2.0 is delegated authorization: the client gets a limited, short-lived token and never sees the user's password.
  • Choose the grant by the client: Authorization Code + PKCE for anything with a user, Client Credentials for services, never ROPC or Implicit.
  • Access tokens go to APIs and live minutes; refresh tokens go only to the Authorization Server; the ID token (OIDC) tells the client who the user is.
  • With asymmetric keys and a JWKS, the gateway validates tokens locally; introspection (like /auth/solve) trades a network hop for immediate revocation.
  • Validation is more than the signature: check exp, iss, aud and scopes — then each service still checks ownership of the data.

  1. HARDT, D. (ed.). RFC 6749 — The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework. IETF, 2012. ↩

  2. LODDERSTEDT, T. et al. RFC 9700 — Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security. IETF, 2025. See also the OAuth 2.1 draft. ↩↩↩

  3. JONES, M.; HARDT, D. RFC 6750 — The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework: Bearer Token Usage. IETF, 2012. ↩

  4. DENNISS, W. et al. RFC 8628 — OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant. IETF, 2019. ↩

  5. SAKIMURA, N. et al. OpenID Connect Core 1.0. OpenID Foundation. ↩↩

  6. SAKIMURA, N.; BRADLEY, J.; AGARWAL, N. RFC 7636 — Proof Key for Code Exchange by OAuth Public Clients. IETF, 2015. ↩

  7. JONES, M. RFC 7517 — JSON Web Key (JWK). IETF, 2015. ↩

  8. SHEFFER, Y.; HARDT, D.; JONES, M. RFC 8725 — JSON Web Token Best Current Practices. IETF, 2020. ↩

  9. RICHER, J. (ed.). RFC 7662 — OAuth 2.0 Token Introspection. IETF, 2015. ↩

items.title: Zero Trust, mTLS & Secrets
items.text: Picture the store running in Kubernetes. A vulnerable JSON library lets an attacker execute code inside one product-service pod. From there, in a classic setup, the attacker can call account-service directly with the header id-account: <any id> and read every customer, connect to Postgres with the password found in the pod's environment variables, and reach any other pod in the cluster — because "inside the cluster" means "trusted". Nothing the gateway does helps: the attacker is already behind it. This page is about limiting what an attacker can do after one component is compromised.

items.title: From perimeter security to Zero Trust
items.text:
Traditional perimeter security (the "castle and moat" model) trusts everything inside the network and blocks everything outside. The problem: once an attacker is inside — via a compromised credential, a vulnerable dependency, or an insider — they can move from machine to machine. This is called lateral movement.

Zero Trust removes the idea of a trusted network. Its principle is "never trust, always verify": every request is authenticated and authorized on its own merits, regardless of where it comes from. Google popularised the model with its BeyondCorp project1, and NIST standardised it in SP 800-2072.

flowchart LR
    subgraph perimeter ["Perimeter model"]
        fw["Firewall"] -->|"trusted zone"| int["Internal services<br>(trust each other implicitly)"]
    end
    subgraph zt ["Zero Trust model"]
        any["Any request<br>(internal or external)"] -->|"identity + context"| pep["Enforcement point<br>(gateway, sidecar)"]
        pep -->|"ask"| pdp["Policy decision"]
        pdp -->|"allow, least privilege"| res["Resource"]
        pdp -->|"deny"| rej["Rejected"]
    end

NIST names the two moving parts: a Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) sits in the path of the request and blocks or forwards it, and a Policy Decision Point (PDP) decides, from identity and context, whether the request is allowed. In the store, the gateway is the PEP for external traffic; inside the cluster, a service-mesh sidecar next to each service plays the same role for internal calls.

items.title: Zero Trust principles
items.text: Principle What it means Mechanisms Verify identity explicitly every user and every workload proves who it is on every request OAuth 2.0 / OIDC tokens, mTLS, SPIFFE Least privilege grant only the access needed, for only as long as needed scopes, RBAC/ABAC, short-lived tokens and credentials Assume breach design as if an attacker is already inside; limit the blast radius micro-segmentation (NetworkPolicy), encryption in transit and at rest Continuous validation trust is re-evaluated, not granted once short token TTLs, re-authentication for sensitive actions, monitoring

items.title: Example: the compromised pod, again
items.text: Attacker step Perimeter model Zero Trust control Section Call account-service with a forged id-account header accepted — the caller is "inside" account-service accepts calls only from the gateway's workload identity (mTLS + authorization policy) mTLS Open a connection to any pod allowed NetworkPolicy allows only declared flows; product-service → account-service is not one of them NetworkPolicy Read the DB password from the environment and use it later works for months a short-lived, per-service credential that expires within the hour Secrets

items.title: Service-to-service identity: mTLS
items.text:
How does product-service know that a call really comes from order-service? An IP address proves nothing — pods are recreated with new IPs, and an attacker can send from any pod. The answer is a cryptographic identity per workload.

  • TLS (Transport Layer Security) — the protocol behind HTTPS. The server presents an X.509 certificate (its public key plus its name, signed by a Certificate Authority, CA); the client verifies it. The channel is encrypted, but the server does not know who the client is.
  • mTLS (mutual TLS) — the server also asks for the client's certificate. Both sides present certificates and verify each other: the channel is encrypted and both identities are proven.
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Order as order-service
    participant CA as SPIRE (workload CA)
    participant Prod as product-service

    Order->>CA: attest workload, request SVID
    CA-->>Order: X.509 SVID: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/store/sa/order-service
    Prod->>CA: attest workload, request SVID
    CA-->>Prod: X.509 SVID
    Order->>Prod: ClientHello
    Prod-->>Order: ServerHello + product cert + CertificateRequest
    Order->>Order: verify product cert against trust bundle
    Order->>Prod: order cert + CertificateVerify (proof of private key)
    Prod->>Prod: verify order cert, read SPIFFE ID
    Note over Order,Prod: encrypted channel + mutual identity

Issuing and rotating certificates by hand for dozens of services does not scale. SPIFFE3 (Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone) standardises a workload identity — a URI such as spiffe://cluster.local/ns/store/sa/order-service — and the SVID (SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Document), a short-lived X.509 certificate carrying it. SPIRE is its reference implementation: it checks (attests) which workload is asking, typically from its Kubernetes service account, and issues certificates that live for about an hour by default and rotate automatically.

Service meshes (Istio, Linkerd) inject a sidecar proxy next to each pod that performs mTLS transparently — no application code changes. Istio derives the identity from the pod's Kubernetes service account in the same SPIFFE format.

items.title: mTLS authenticates; a policy authorizes
items.text:
mTLS proves who is calling; it does not decide whether the caller may call. That is an authorization policy, evaluated by the sidecar on every request. With Istio4, allowing only order-service to read products looks like this:

apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: product-allow-order
  namespace: store
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: product-service
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
    - from:
        - source:
            principals: ["cluster.local/ns/store/sa/order-service"]
      to:
        - operation:
            methods: ["GET"]
            paths: ["/products/*"]

Once a workload has at least one ALLOW policy, requests that match none of its rules are denied.

items.title: Network segmentation with NetworkPolicy
items.text:
A Kubernetes NetworkPolicy5 is a firewall rule for pods: it selects pods by label and lists which other pods (or namespaces, or IP ranges) may connect to them, on which ports. It works at layers 3/4 (IP and port), so it complements mTLS: even if an attacker steals a certificate, the network refuses connections that were never declared.

The recommended pattern is default deny, then allow explicitly. First, deny all ingress to every pod in the namespace:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-ingress
  namespace: store
spec:
  podSelector: {}        # all pods in the namespace
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress            # no ingress rules listed = nothing allowed

Then open each legitimate flow. This policy allows only gateway-service pods to reach order-service on port 8080:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: order-service-ingress
  namespace: store
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: order-service
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: gateway-service
      ports:
        - port: 8080

Policies are additive: a pod selected by any policy accepts only the traffic that at least one policy allows. A podSelector inside from matches pods in the same namespace; to allow another namespace, add a namespaceSelector.

A NetworkPolicy only works if the network plugin enforces it

The Kubernetes API accepts NetworkPolicy objects on any cluster, but they are enforced by the CNI (network) plugin. Calico and Cilium enforce them; the default minikube network does not, so the policy is silently ignored. To try it in Hands-on 5, start the cluster with minikube start --cni=calico.

items.title: Secrets management
items.text:
A secret is any value that grants access: database passwords, the JWT_SECRET_KEY of Hands-on 3, API keys, the Docker Hub token of Hands-on 4, private keys. Secrets must not live in source code, container images, or plain configuration — anything that gets copied, versioned, or logged.

Kubernetes Secrets are base64, not encrypted

A Kubernetes Secret stores data as base64-encoded strings. Base64 is encoding, not encryption — the Postgres secret of Hands-on 5 decodes in one command:

echo c3RvcmU= | base64 -d        # prints: store
kubectl get secret postgres-secrets -o jsonpath='{.data.POSTGRES_PASSWORD}' | base64 -d

Anyone allowed to read Secrets in the namespace — or to create a pod there that mounts them — can read them all. By default they are also stored unencrypted in etcd, and a secrets.yaml committed to Git is public to everyone with access to the repository6.

Minimum hygiene for native Secrets: enable encryption at rest for etcd7, restrict get/list on Secrets with RBAC, and keep secret manifests out of Git (or commit them only encrypted, e.g. with Sealed Secrets or SOPS). Beyond that, use an external secrets manager:

Approach Pros Cons Kubernetes Secrets simple, native base64 only; needs encryption at rest and RBAC discipline Cloud secret managers (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager) managed, automatic rotation, audit log tied to one cloud; extra latency HashiCorp Vault dynamic secrets, any cloud or on-prem, fine-grained audit operational overhead

Tools such as the External Secrets Operator synchronise values from a cloud manager or Vault into native Secrets, so applications keep reading them the usual way.

HashiCorp Vault introduces dynamic secrets8: instead of storing one long-lived database password shared by every replica, Vault creates a short-lived, unique database user for each requester, with a lease (for example, one hour). When the lease expires, Vault drops the user. A password stolen from a compromised pod stops working on its own, and the audit log shows exactly which pod used which credential.

The Vault Agent Injector pattern adds a sidecar that authenticates to Vault with the pod's service account and writes the secret into a file — here /vault/secrets/db — which the application reads; the credential never appears in the pod spec, a ConfigMap, or an environment variable9:

annotations:
  vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject: "true"
  vault.hashicorp.com/role: "order-service"
  vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-secret-db: "database/creds/order-service"

Common mistakes

  • Secrets in Git, even in a private repository or "just for the dev environment" — history keeps them forever; rotate any secret that was ever committed.
  • One shared credential for every service — when it leaks you cannot tell who used it, and rotating it breaks everyone at once.
  • Secrets in logs and error messages — mask them, as Jenkins does with withCredentials.
  • Treating mTLS as authorization — a valid certificate proves identity, not permission; add an authorization policy.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Zero Trust drops the "trusted internal network": every request, internal or external, carries an identity and is checked against a policy (PEP + PDP).
  • Design for assume breach: limit what a compromised pod can reach (NetworkPolicy), call (authorization policy) and read (short-lived secrets).
  • mTLS gives each workload a cryptographic identity; SPIFFE/SPIRE or a service mesh issue and rotate those certificates automatically.
  • NetworkPolicy should start from default deny, and it only works with a CNI that enforces it.
